articles.title: I Let AI Build a Feature Without Giving It the Full Context
articles.description: If you give an AI a vague prompt, it will give you a confident answer. And that confidence will cost...
articles.body_html:
If you give an AI a vague prompt, it will give you a confident answer. And that confidence will cost you a weekend of debugging.

Last month I decided to test how far I could push an AI agent. I didn't want to use it to write a simple function. I wanted it to build an entire backend feature from scratch, end-to-end.

The feature was a standard requirement: A CSV export endpoint for user data.

I opened my AI tool, cracked my knuckles, and typed a prompt that took me exactly 5 seconds to write:

"Create an Express API endpoint that exports all user records from the database into a CSV file and returns it for download."

Thirty seconds later, the AI spat out a perfectly formatted controller, a well-written database query, and even a utility function to convert JSON to CSV. It looked elegant. The variable names were clean. It compiled immediately.

I felt like a 10x developer. I pushed the code, merged the PR, and deployed to production.

And then, within 10 minutes, the support tickets started rolling in.

The Illusion of Perfect AI Code

Here is the thing about AI: It doesn't know what it doesn't know.

Because I didn't give the AI any context about our system, it made three massive assumptions that completely broke production:

1. The All Users Security Nightmare

I wrote "exports all user records." The AI did exactly that. But wait I work on a multi-tenant SaaS. "All users" means every single user across every single company in our database.
An admin from Company A downloaded the CSV and suddenly had the names and emails of Company B. It was a massive data leak because I forgot to tell the AI, "Only export users belonging to the authenticated user's organization."

2. The Memory Explosion (OOM)

The AI wrote a beautiful query: const users = await db.user.findMany(); followed by mapping over the array. It worked perfectly in local testing where I had 50 users.
In production, we had 2.5 million users. The server didn't just crash; it had an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error because the AI tried to load 2.5 million records into memory simultaneously. I forgot to tell the AI, "Use a streaming approach or pagination."

3. The CSV Injection Vulnerability

The AI did a simple join(',') to create the CSV. But users can enter their own names. If a user named themselves =SUM(1+1) or =cmd|' /C calc'!A0, Excel would actually execute that formula when the admin opened the CSV file. I forgot to tell the AI, "Sanitize the data to prevent CSV injection."

None of these bugs were the AI's fault. The AI did exactly what I asked.

The failure was 100% mine, because I gave the AI the "What" but not the "Where" and the "How."

The Context Debt is Real

This experiment taught me one massive lesson: AI is not a mind reader. It is an incredibly fast, highly obedient intern with amnesia.

When you don't give the AI the full context of your system, its architectural rules, and your security boundaries, it writes code in a vacuum. And code written in a vacuum is just technical debt waiting to explode in production.

We spend so much time arguing about which AI model is smarter GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Llama 3. But a smarter model wouldn't have saved me here. Even a genius model can't guess that I'm using a multi-tenant database with millions of rows.

How to Fix It: Context-Driven Development

If you want AI to actually save you time (and not get you fired), you have to stop writing Twitter-style prompts and start writing Context-Rich prompts.

Here are the 3 rules I now follow:

1. Share the Database Schema

Don't just say "user data." Paste your Prisma schema, your TypeORM entities, or your SQL table definitions into the prompt. AI is amazing at spotting relations when it can actually see the tenant_id foreign key.

2. State the Constraints Explicitly

If your system has rules, write them down.
"Assume the table has 2 million rows. Use a streaming approach."
"This is a multi-tenant app. Always filter by organization ID."

3. Define the Edge Cases Before You Prompt

Tell the AI to be paranoid.
"Assume users can input malicious strings. Sanitize all CSV outputs."
"Add rate limiting to this endpoint."

The Ultimate Question: Prompts vs. Models?

We are living in a golden era of AI models. They are getting exponentially smarter every six months. But my production incident proved that a brilliant model with terrible context is still a disaster.

So, I want to ask you:

Is better prompting more important than better AI models?

Will we eventually reach a point where AI knows our codebases so well (via RAG and local indexing) that we don't need to prompt perfectly? Or is "Context Engineering" the real skill of the future?

Drop your thoughts in the comments below. I'd love to know how you handle giving AI the right context!

articles.title: Your Database Has Backups. Have You Ever Tried Restoring One?
articles.description: Your backup job ran successfully last night.  This morning, a migration deleted the wrong data.  You...
articles.body_html:
Your backup job ran successfully last night.

This morning, a migration deleted the wrong data.

You open the backup dashboard. Everything is green.

Then someone asks:

“How long until the app works again?”

That’s when you discover whether you have a recovery process—or just backup files.

A successful backup is important. Restoring it and checking the application gives you much stronger evidence that you can recover.

Here’s a practical drill you can run before an incident makes it urgent.

1. Define what you need to recover

Start with a specific scenario:

“Our main database is unavailable. We need to restore the application using an existing backup.”

Write down two targets:

Recovery Time Objective (RTO): How long can the service be unavailable?

Recovery Point Objective (RPO): How much recent data can you afford to lose, measured in time?

For example:

Recovery time target: 60 minutes
Acceptable data-loss window: 15 minutes

These are examples, not universal recommendations. Choose targets based on what your users and business can tolerate.

AWS recommends performing recovery tests to validate whether your backup process meets these objectives.

2. Restore an existing backup into an isolated environment

Use a backup produced by your normal process. Creating a special export for the drill can hide problems in the process you actually depend on.

Restore into a separate database or environment with a clearly different name:

app_restore_drill

Check the destination before running restore commands.

Also isolate the recovered application from production integrations. You don’t want a test worker sending real invoices, emails, or payment requests.

Protect restored customer data with appropriate access controls, and remove the test environment when the exercise is complete.

Google Cloud’s recovery guidance recommends testing backups in a non-production environment.

3. Check whether you have everything the restore needs

Finding the backup file is only the beginning.

Can you access:

  • The backup storage account?
  • Required decryption keys?
  • Compatible database tooling?
  • Necessary extensions?
  • Database roles and permissions?
  • Application configuration?

For PostgreSQL, a single-database pg_dump does not include cluster-wide objects such as roles and tablespaces. Those need a separate recovery plan; PostgreSQL provides pg_dumpall for global objects.

This is exactly the kind of missing dependency a drill should reveal.

4. Inspect the restored data

A completed restore command doesn’t prove that you recovered the right data.

Check important business records:

  • Can you find a known customer?
  • Are their orders or invoices present?
  • Do payment totals match the expected state?
  • Are relationships between records intact?
  • Are permissions behaving correctly?

Compare against the backup’s expected recovery point. A backup from midnight won’t contain an order created at 9 a.m.

Use known transactions or recovery markers where possible. A single timestamp or total row count can miss problems.

Verify the data your application depends on, not merely the existence of its tables.

5. Start the application against the restored database

Now test the recovered application.

Can a test user sign in?

Can they open an existing record?

Can they create and update a new record?

Can the application generate an important report?

This can expose problems that database checks alone miss:

  • Missing permissions.
  • Unavailable extensions.
  • An incompatible application version.
  • Incorrect connection settings.
  • Missing files referenced by database records.

Your database might contain a document’s filename while the actual document lives in object storage.

Recovering the database is one part of recovering the service.

Check the other stateful dependencies your application needs.

6. Measure the whole recovery

Start the timer when you begin the recovery procedure.

Include time spent:

  1. Finding and accessing the backup.
  2. Preparing the environment.
  3. Restoring data.
  4. Configuring the application.
  5. Validating important workflows.

Stop when the service reaches your defined recovery criteria.

Record which incident stages the drill did not simulate, such as detection, escalation, or production traffic cutover.

You might discover:

Database restore: 12 minutes
Environment and application setup: 25 minutes
Validation: 18 minutes

Total drill time: 55 minutes

Reporting only the 12-minute restore would hide most of the work.

7. Measure the data-loss window honestly

Suppose an incident happens at 10 a.m., but the latest recoverable state is midnight.

That leaves a ten-hour gap.

A successful restore doesn’t make that gap acceptable.

If your target is 15 minutes, your backup strategy needs to support a sufficiently recent recovery point.

Depending on the database and platform, that may involve more frequent backups, transaction-log archiving, or point-in-time recovery.

Also distinguish the failure you’re testing:

  • If the database disappears, you want a recent recoverable state.
  • If a bad change corrupts data, you need a recoverable state before that change.

Newer isn’t always the correct recovery point.

8. Write instructions another person can follow

Document the process while you perform it.

Include:

  • Where backups are stored.
  • How authorized people obtain access.
  • Which tools and versions are required.
  • How to select the recovery point.
  • How to identify the restore destination.
  • How to validate the result.
  • Who makes the decision to return the service to users.

Keep credentials in your approved secret-management system, rather than copying them into the document.

Then have another team member follow the instructions.

If they need to ask you about several undocumented steps, you’ve found useful improvements.

A small recovery report

Your first report can be simple:

Scenario:
Main database unavailable.

Backup used:
Identifier and expected recovery point.

Restore destination:
Isolated drill environment.

Validation:
Sign-in, record lookup, create/update, reporting.

Measured recovery time:
55 minutes.

Observed recovery point:
Recorded and compared with the data-loss target.

Problems:
Missing role setup and outdated configuration instructions.

Follow-up:
Automate role provisioning and update the runbook.

Repeat the drill after fixing the gaps. Schedule future exercises according to the importance of the service and changes to its infrastructure.

Before your next deployment

Ask your team:

“When did we last restore a backup and run the application against it?”

If the answer is “never,” you’ve found a valuable engineering task.

Start small: restore one existing backup, validate one important workflow, and record what happened.

The first drill doesn’t need to be perfect. It needs to reveal what would otherwise surprise you during an incident.

Have you ever restored a backup that looked healthy but wasn’t enough to recover the application?

Further reading

  • AWS: Periodically recover data to verify backup integrity and processes
  • Google Cloud: Test recovery from data loss
  • PostgreSQL: Backup and restore

articles.title: FastAPI 0.162.0 fixes a required checkbox that was never actually required
articles.description: FastAPI 0.162.0 stopped silently turning every omitted boolean form field into False, including ones declared Form(...) as required. I measured the before and after on four field shapes, and found an unrelated sibling-parameter break that shipped the same week.
articles.body_html:
I wrote a sign-up endpoint with a required consent checkbox: agree_tos: bool = Form(...). I submitted the form without ticking it. The request went through anyway, with agree_tos recorded as False, HTTP 200. No validation error, no indication that a field I had explicitly marked required was missing.

That is FastAPI 0.161.1, released 22 October 2026. One release later, 0.162.0, released the following day, the same request gets rejected with a proper 422. I wanted to know exactly what changed, what else it touched, and what shipped alongside it that nobody is talking about yet.

What actually changed

FastAPI's own changelog for 0.162.0 describes it as restoring "default handling for omitted boolean form fields," so that FastAPI "no longer infers False for omitted booleans." Before this release, any boolean field submitted via a form, whether a single Form() parameter or a boolean field nested in a Pydantic model used with Form(), was coerced to False the moment it was missing from the multipart body. It didn't matter what you'd actually declared as the default, or whether you'd declared a default at all.

I set up two virtual environments, one pinned to fastapi==0.161.1 and one to fastapi==0.162.0, both running identical Pydantic (2.14.2) and Starlette (1.10.0) versions so the only variable was FastAPI itself. Then I sent the same requests, with the field simply absent, to three declarations:

Field declaration 0.161.1 0.162.0
subscribe: bool = Form(False) {"subscribe": false}, 200 {"subscribe": false}, 200
remember_me: bool = Form(True) {"remember_me": false}, 200 {"remember_me": true}, 200
agree_tos: bool = Form(...) (required) {"agree_tos": false}, 200 422 Field required

The first row is unaffected because False is both the declared default and the buggy fallback, so the two happen to agree. The second row is where the bug becomes visible: a field with an explicit default of True quietly became False on every request that left it out, which is backwards from what Form(True) is supposed to mean. The third row is the one I'd actually worry about. Declaring a field required with Form(...) is supposed to mean the client must send it. On 0.161.1, that constraint simply didn't exist for booleans — the field was always "present," just always False.

This isn't limited to standalone Form() parameters. I built a small Pydantic model, PersonForm, with newsletter: bool = True, and submitted it via person: PersonForm = Form() with the newsletter field left out entirely:

-- 0.161.1 --
{"name":"Alex","newsletter":false}
-- 0.162.0 --
{"name":"Alex","newsletter":true}

Same bug, same fix, inside a model rather than a bare parameter. Anyone validating boolean preferences through a form model, not just loose parameters, was affected.

The part that should worry you more than a wrong default

A default silently flipping from True to False is an annoyance. A Form(...) boolean silently accepting omission is a different category of problem, because Form(...) is the explicit, documented way to say "this field is not optional." If your consent checkbox, your "I have read the pricing," or any other compliance-shaped boolean was wired up as a required form field on a 0.16x release before 0.162.0, submitting the form without ticking the box did not fail. It succeeded, with the box recorded as unticked. Whether that's a real compliance gap depends on what you built on top of it, but the API contract you thought you had — "the client must send this" — was not being enforced for this one type.

I don't know how far back this regression goes; the changelog's own word is "restore," which implies this worked correctly at some earlier point before a regression reintroduced it. I only tested 0.161.1 against 0.162.0, so I can only speak to that specific boundary, not the full history.

An unrelated breaking change shipped the same week

While pulling release notes to understand 0.162.0, I noticed 0.160.0, released the day before, carries its own entry in FastAPI's Breaking Changes section: parameter models now apply their own extra setting to sibling fields in the same location, not just to their own fields.

I built an endpoint with a query parameter model configured with extra="forbid", alongside a completely separate sort query parameter declared on the same route, outside that model:

class FilterParams(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    q: str
    limit: int = 10

@app.get("/search")
def search(filters: FilterParams = Query(), sort: str = Query("relevance")):
    ...

On fastapi==0.159.1, a request with q, limit, and sort all present returns 200 — sort belongs to a different parameter, so FilterParams's extra="forbid" has nothing to say about it. On fastapi==0.162.0, the identical request is rejected:

{"detail":[{"type":"extra_forbidden","loc":["query","sort"],
"msg":"Extra inputs are not permitted","input":"newest"}]}

sort is a legitimately declared, separately named parameter on the same endpoint. It is not extra by any definition a reader of the route signature would guess. The new behaviour treats "forbid extras" on one model as "forbid anything not explicitly inside this model," which now reaches across to parameters that were never part of it. If you have any endpoint combining a strict (extra="forbid") parameter model with other loose parameters, upgrading past 0.160.0 will start rejecting requests that used to be valid, with no code change on your end. I checked this is intentional, documented behaviour as of 0.160.0's changelog, not a bug report waiting to happen, but it's the kind of change that's easy to miss if you only read the 0.162.0 entry because that's the one with the catchy "booleans" headline.

What didn't break

The same week also shipped support for combining unions of form models (0.161.0), which lets a single endpoint accept either of two differently shaped form bodies. I tested this with a card-payment model and a bank-payment model as alternatives on one endpoint. Both versions handled valid submissions of either shape correctly, and both produced the same structured, per-branch 422 when neither shape matched:

{"detail":[
  {"loc":["body","CardPayment","card_number"],"msg":"Field required", ...},
  {"loc":["body","BankPayment","iban"],"msg":"Field required", ...}
]}

I was checking for a regression here precisely because it shipped in the same burst of releases as the two breaking changes above, and it would have been easy to assume everything from that week was suspect. It wasn't. This feature worked identically before and after 0.162.0.

I also checked one documented claim directly: FastAPI's own docs say a checked HTML checkbox sends the string "on", and that FastAPI accepts "on" as True. Sending subscribe=on explicitly returned {"subscribe": true} on both 0.161.1 and 0.162.0. That part of the documentation held up in both versions; it's the omitted-field path the docs don't mention at all, which is exactly where the bug lived.

Finally, since a validation bug and a blocking I/O bug look very different under load, I fired 50 concurrent requests at the required-boolean endpoint on 0.162.0 with the field omitted. All 50 came back 422. Nothing about the fix is dependent on timing or request ordering — it's a straightforward default-resolution change, not a race condition that only shows up occasionally.

What I got wrong on the way

I didn't start today testing FastAPI. My original plan was Kubernetes 1.36's user namespaces feature, which went GA this year and lets a pod run as root inside its container while mapping to an unprivileged UID on the host. I installed kind and tried to bring up a kindest/node:v1.36.4 cluster to test it against a real pod.

kubeadm init timed out waiting on the control plane, and stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup told me why: this machine runs cgroup v1, which newer kubelets refuse to boot on without a manual override. I have that override documented from testing it on this exact host before. But applying it wouldn't have been enough — a kind cluster on this machine also can't actually start containerised workloads at all, failing with runc create failed: unable to start container process: can't get final child's PID from pipe: EOF, a sandboxing limit on nested containers that exists independently of the cgroup version. A cluster that can't schedule a single real pod isn't a useful place to test namespace mapping on actual containers, so I abandoned it rather than publish something I couldn't actually observe happening.

Run it yourself

This needs only python3 and pip; no Docker, no account.

python3 -m venv old && old/bin/pip install -q "fastapi==0.161.1" "uvicorn[standard]" python-multipart
python3 -m venv new && new/bin/pip install -q "fastapi==0.162.0" "uvicorn[standard]" python-multipart

cat > app.py <<'EOF'
from fastapi import FastAPI, Form
app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/remember-me")
def remember_me(remember_me: bool = Form(True)):
    return {"remember_me": remember_me}

@app.post("/agree")
def agree(agree_tos: bool = Form(...)):
    return {"agree_tos": agree_tos}
EOF
cp app.py old/app.py && cp app.py new/app.py

old/bin/uvicorn --app-dir old app:app --port 8101 &
new/bin/uvicorn --app-dir new app:app --port 8102 &
sleep 2

echo "old, default True, field omitted:"; curl -s -X POST localhost:8101/remember-me -F "x=1"
echo "new, default True, field omitted:"; curl -s -X POST localhost:8102/remember-me -F "x=1"
echo "old, required, field omitted:"; curl -s -X POST localhost:8101/agree -F "x=1"
echo "new, required, field omitted:"; curl -s -X POST localhost:8102/agree -F "x=1"

kill %1 %2

On my machine that printed {"remember_me":false} then {"remember_me":true}, followed by {"agree_tos":false} then the 422 field-required error. Same four outcomes as the table further up, from a nine-line app rather than the fuller one I tested against.

What to do with this

Run pip show fastapi on whatever's actually deployed before you take any of this on faith. Then grep your routes for Form(...) next to a bool type hint, or a Pydantic form model with an unannotated boolean field — grep -rn "bool.*Form(\.\.\.)" gets you most of the way there. A consent checkbox, a "ship without insurance" toggle, anything where the absence of a tick was supposed to be rejected rather than silently recorded as False. On anything before 0.162.0, that rejection never happened, and your test suite almost certainly didn't catch it, because the field was always present in the response, just always false.

The other change needs the opposite kind of check, not for missing enforcement but for enforcement you didn't ask for. Find any extra="forbid" parameter model sharing a route with other loose parameters, and send it a request using one of those other parameters the way a client already does in production. If 0.160.0 or later rejects it, that's not a bug to file upstream — pull the parameter into the model, or drop forbid for ignore, because the FastAPI maintainers consider the current behaviour correct.

articles.title: Your Website Has a Design System. Does Your Marketing Team Have a Content System?
articles.description: A marketing content system gives your team a reliable way to create, organize, update, and publish...
articles.body_html:
A marketing content system gives your team a reliable way to create, organize, update, and publish website content. Your design system may already define colors, typography, buttons, spacing, and reusable page components. But those rules don't explain who owns a landing page, how messaging stays consistent, or what happens when five people need to update different parts of the website.

This gap becomes noticeable as a company grows. Marketing adds new campaigns, product teams introduce features, and the website accumulates more pages, messages, and calls to action. Everyone has access to the same design components, but content decisions still happen across scattered documents, Slack conversations, spreadsheets, and individual work habits.

The result can be a website that looks consistent but communicates inconsistently. A marketing team might have all the right components and still struggle to keep messaging accurate, update pages quickly, or coordinate changes across the site.

That is where a marketing content system becomes useful. It gives the people responsible for the website a shared way to manage the content that goes into those carefully designed components.

TL;DR

A design system keeps the visual and interface elements of your website consistent, while a marketing content system helps your team manage the words, messaging, ownership, and publishing processes behind those pages. It defines how content is created, reviewed, reused, updated, and maintained. Together, these systems help marketing teams publish faster, keep messaging aligned, and manage website changes with fewer bottlenecks.

A Design System Solves a Different Problem

A design system gives your website a shared visual language. It defines how components should look and behave, so teams can build new pages without inventing every interface element from scratch.

For example, a typical design system might include:

  • Typography rules for headings, body text, and labels.
  • Standard buttons, forms, navigation, and cards.
  • Reusable page sections and layout patterns.
  • Spacing, color, and accessibility guidelines.
  • Component documentation for designers and developers.

Established design systems such as the Atlassian Design System demonstrate how shared components, design foundations, and documentation help teams create consistent digital experiences.

These standards help maintain a consistent experience across the website. A new landing page can use the same button styles, form patterns, and page layouts as the rest of the site.

However, the design system doesn't automatically tell your team what those components should communicate. It won't decide which product benefit belongs in a hero section, who approves a pricing-page change, or when an outdated customer quote needs replacing.

Consider a company with several product pages. Each page uses the same heading styles, card layouts, and CTA buttons. Visually, everything feels connected. Yet one page describes a feature using an old product name, another promotes a benefit that has changed, and a third uses messaging that the sales team stopped using months ago.

The components are consistent. The content is not.

This is an ownership and content-management problem. Solving it requires a system that covers the information inside the components, along with the people and processes responsible for keeping that information accurate.

What a Marketing Content System Actually Covers

A marketing content system defines how website content is managed throughout its lifecycle. It connects content decisions with the workflows, responsibilities, and technical setup that support the website.

It doesn't need to be a new platform or a complicated collection of documents. For many B2B SaaS teams, it can start with clear content standards, documented ownership, reusable content patterns, and a reliable publishing process.

A practical marketing content system should cover four areas:

1. Content structure and standards

Define how your team writes and organizes website content. This includes product terminology, messaging guidelines, heading conventions, CTA language, tone of voice, and rules for describing features.

2. Reusable content patterns

Document recurring content structures, such as hero sections, feature descriptions, customer proof, pricing explanations, and FAQ blocks. Teams should know which patterns are available and how to use them without creating inconsistent variations.

3. Ownership and review responsibilities

Make it clear who writes, reviews, approves, and maintains each type of content. Product marketing may own feature messaging, while a marketing lead approves campaign positioning. Developers may support technical implementation without becoming the default approvers of every content change.

4. Publishing and maintenance workflows

Establish how content moves from a draft to a live page. Include review requirements, publishing permissions, update procedures, and checks for links, forms, tracking, and page behavior.

These four areas work together. Content standards help people make consistent decisions, reusable patterns reduce unnecessary work, ownership prevents approval confusion, and publishing workflows make sure approved changes reach the website safely.

The goal is simple: give your marketing team a dependable way to manage website content as the company, product, and website continue to grow.

Why Content Ownership Becomes Difficult as a Website Grows

When a company has only a few website pages, content ownership can feel straightforward. A marketer writes the copy, someone reviews it, and a developer publishes the update if technical help is needed.

That process becomes harder as the website expands. New product pages, campaign landing pages, customer stories, integration pages, and resource libraries introduce more content owners and more opportunities for conflicting information.

A product marketer might update a feature description while the website team is preparing a new landing page. Sales might request a change to the messaging on a pricing page, while another team is updating the same product terminology across several pages. Without clear ownership, these changes can move forward independently and create inconsistencies.

The problem isn't that too many people contribute to the website. Different teams have useful information to share. The problem is that nobody has a clear view of who is responsible for the final content and how related changes should be coordinated.

A content system should establish ownership at two levels:

Content ownership: Who is responsible for the accuracy of the information? Product marketing may own feature descriptions, while sales or customer success can provide feedback on customer-facing language.

Publishing ownership: Who can approve and publish the change? A marketing lead might approve the messaging, while an authorized website editor handles publication. Technical changes that affect templates, integrations, or site functionality may still require developer review.

This distinction helps teams avoid unnecessary approval delays while keeping the right people involved. Marketing can manage routine content updates within agreed permissions, and developers can focus on changes that genuinely require technical work.

It also makes ongoing maintenance easier. When a product feature changes, the team knows who should review the related website content and which pages may need updating.

Build Reusable Content Patterns Your Team Can Actually Maintain

A design system gives teams reusable interface components. A marketing content system should give them reusable content patterns too.

Think about how often a B2B SaaS website explains the same types of information. Product pages describe features and benefits. Integration pages explain compatibility and use cases. Landing pages introduce an offer, provide supporting evidence, and guide visitors toward a CTA.

If every page starts from a blank document, marketers spend time solving the same structural problems repeatedly. The result can also vary significantly across pages, even when they serve similar purposes.

Reusable content patterns provide a shared starting point. They define the information a page section should communicate while leaving room for the details of each product, audience, or campaign.

For example, a feature section could follow a consistent structure:

  • Feature name: What the capability is called.
  • Customer problem: What difficulty it addresses.
  • Practical benefit: How it helps the customer.
  • Supporting evidence: A product detail, example, or customer result.
  • Next step: The action visitors can take to learn more.

This structure helps writers produce complete, useful content. It also gives reviewers a consistent way to evaluate whether a section explains the feature clearly.

The same principle applies to other recurring sections, including customer testimonials, integration descriptions, pricing explanations, and FAQ content.

However, reusable patterns need ownership and maintenance. A template that contains outdated product terminology or an old CTA can spread the same mistake across multiple pages. Each pattern should have a clear purpose, documented usage guidance, and an owner responsible for keeping it accurate.

Your website CMS may already support reusable blocks, structured content fields, or shared page templates. These capabilities can support the system, provided the team documents how and when to use them.

Connect Content Management to Your Website Workflow

Even with clear standards and ownership, a content system can fail if it doesn't connect to the way website changes actually get published.

A new landing page might have excellent copy and an approved design, but it still needs a publishing process. Someone must check the page structure, verify links and forms, confirm tracking, and make sure the final page works across devices.

This is where content operations and WebOps meet. Content decisions need a reliable path to production, with enough checks to protect the website without making every small update a development project.

Define a Clear Marketing Content System Workflow

A practical workflow can follow five stages:

1. Request: Define the page or content change, its purpose, target audience, owner, and expected outcome.

2. Create: Write or update the content using the team's messaging standards and reusable patterns.

3. Review: Ask the relevant stakeholders to check accuracy, positioning, terminology, and any required approvals.

4. Publish: Move the approved content to the live website through the appropriate CMS permissions and publishing process.

5. Verify: Check the published page, links, forms, analytics events, responsive layout, and other requirements affected by the change.

Match the Review Process to the Scope of the Change

Not every content update needs the same level of review. Correcting a typo doesn't require the same process as changing product positioning across several landing pages. Your workflow should reflect the risk and scope of the change.

For example, a simple headline correction may only need a content owner and a quick live-page check. A new pricing page may require product, marketing, and technical reviews, followed by more extensive testing.

The important part is making these expectations clear before work begins. Marketing should know which updates it can publish independently, which changes require approval, and when engineering needs to get involved.

This is closely connected to the wider challenge of keeping marketing website requests from getting stuck in development backlogs. A defined content workflow helps teams submit clearer requests, handle routine updates efficiently, and give developers the context they need when technical work is necessary.

Keep Your Content System Accurate as the Website Evolves

A content system needs regular maintenance. Product features change, positioning evolves, campaigns end, and customer expectations shift. Without a process for reviewing existing pages, even a well-organized website can gradually become inconsistent.

This is why content maintenance should be part of normal website operations. Teams need to know which pages contain important product information, who owns them, and when they should be reviewed.

Build a Regular Website Content Review Process

A few practical habits can help:

Assign an owner to important pages. Every key product, pricing, integration, and conversion page should have someone responsible for its accuracy. That person doesn't need to make every edit, but they should know when the content needs attention.

Record important content changes. Keep a simple history of significant updates, including what changed, who approved it, and when it went live. This makes it easier to investigate outdated messaging or understand why a page looks different from an earlier version.

Review content after product changes. When a feature is renamed, a pricing model changes, or a product capability is updated, identify the website pages that describe it. Product documentation and website messaging should not drift apart.

Set review dates for high-impact pages. Pricing pages, product pages, and pages used in active campaigns deserve more frequent attention than older resources that receive little traffic. A review schedule helps teams prioritize the content that matters most.

Remove outdated content carefully. Before archiving a page or deleting an old campaign, check its traffic, backlinks, search visibility, and existing links from other pages. Some content may need an update or redirect to preserve its value.

Connect Content Maintenance to Overall Website Health

These practices also connect to broader website maintenance. As I explain in The Hidden Cost of Website Neglect at Growing Tech Companies, small website issues can accumulate and affect performance, lead generation, and the experience visitors receive.

The same principle applies to content. A page that hasn't been reviewed in months may still be live, indexed, and influencing a potential customer's decision. Regular ownership and review help prevent those problems from becoming part of the normal website experience.

How to Know Whether Your Marketing Content System Is Working

A content system should make website management easier to measure. If the team introduces new guidelines and workflows but cannot tell whether they improve day-to-day work, it's difficult to know what needs adjustment.

Start with a few operational measures that reflect how your team manages content.

Metric What it helps you understand
Time from content request to publication How efficiently updates move through the workflow
Number of revisions per update Whether requests and content guidelines are clear
Approval time Where reviews create delays
Outdated pages identified Whether content maintenance is catching neglected information
Publishing errors Whether quality checks are preventing mistakes
Reuse of approved content patterns Whether teams are making effective use of existing structures

These metrics need context. A complex pricing-page update will naturally take longer than a small copy correction. The goal isn't to make every update follow the same timeline. It's to identify unnecessary delays, repeated work, and recurring problems.

For example, if simple landing page changes consistently wait several days for technical approval, the team may need clearer publishing permissions. If reviewers repeatedly request the same messaging corrections, the content standards may need more specific examples.

You can also connect operational improvements to website performance. Track relevant outcomes such as landing page conversion rates, form completion, engagement with important pages, and organic search traffic. These measures won't prove that a content system caused every improvement, but they can help show whether better content management supports the wider marketing goals.

The best system is one your team can actually follow. Start with a few useful standards and responsibilities, review how they work in practice, and improve the process as the website grows.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a marketing content system?
A marketing content system is a set of standards, responsibilities, reusable patterns, and workflows that helps a team create, manage, publish, and maintain website content consistently. It gives everyone a clearer understanding of how content decisions are made and who is responsible for them.

What is the difference between a design system and a content system?
A design system defines the visual and functional components of a website, including typography, colors, buttons, and layouts. A content system manages the information inside those components, including messaging, terminology, content ownership, review processes, and publishing rules. Both systems work together to create a consistent website experience.

Does a marketing content system require a new CMS?
No. A new CMS isn't necessary for most teams. Your existing CMS may already support reusable blocks, structured content, editorial permissions, and publishing workflows. The first step is to establish clear standards and ownership, then identify whether your current tools support those requirements.

Who should own a company's website content?
Ownership should be shared according to expertise and responsibility. Product marketing can manage product messaging, demand generation can own campaign content, and designated marketing leads can approve broader website changes. Developers should handle technical implementation and changes that affect website functionality.

How can a content system help marketing teams publish faster?
A content system reduces repeated decisions and unnecessary approval delays. Reusable content patterns give writers a starting point, clear ownership prevents confusion, and documented publishing permissions help teams handle routine updates without waiting for developers. Technical reviews remain available for changes that require engineering work.

Final Thoughts

Your website's design system gives every page a consistent visual foundation. Your marketing content system gives the people managing those pages a consistent way to work.

As a B2B SaaS website grows, content ownership, messaging, and publishing become harder to coordinate. Without clear processes, even a well-designed website can accumulate outdated information, inconsistent product descriptions, and unnecessary publishing delays.

You don't need a complicated platform to address this. Start by documenting your content standards, assigning owners to important pages, creating reusable content patterns, and defining how updates move from request to publication.

Then connect those practices to your existing website operations and review them as the business evolves.

A well-managed website needs both systems. One keeps the experience consistent for visitors; the other helps your team keep that experience accurate and useful.

articles.title: My homepage took 8 seconds to load. I threw a CDN, a cache, and lazy-loading at it. It was still slow.
articles.description: My homepage took eight seconds to load. Eight full seconds of a spinner — long enough to make tea,...
articles.body_html:
My homepage took eight seconds to load. Eight full seconds of a spinner — long enough to make tea, long enough that anyone on a phone on a train had already closed the tab and forgotten we existed.

So I did what you do. I made it faster. I put a CDN in front of it. I added a caching layer. I lazy-loaded the images, code-split the bundle, slapped a loading skeleton over the blank screen so at least it felt like something was happening. I spent the better part of a month adding fast things to a slow site.

It was still slow. Not quite eight seconds anymore — but nowhere near fast, and worse, I was out of fast things to add. I had bolted every optimization I knew onto the outside of the app, and the app just sat there, taking its time, completely indifferent to all of them.

The month I spent making it faster taught me almost nothing. The afternoon I finally spent understanding why it was slow fixed it. And the gap between those two things turned out to be the whole point.

The pile of fast things

Here's the part I'm a little embarrassed by, because it's such a tell.

Every single thing I added was a reasonable thing to add. A CDN is good. Caching is good. Lazy-loading images is good. Code-splitting is good. None of it was wrong. If you'd looked at my list of changes, you'd have nodded along — that's the performance checklist, that's what you're supposed to do.

But look at what the list actually is. Every item on it is a way to make work happen faster, or closer to the user, or later. Not one of them is "do less work." I had a page that was doing an enormous amount of unnecessary work, and my entire response was to find faster and faster ways to do the unnecessary work. A CDN so the wasted bytes arrive from a nearer city. A cache so I only have to do the pointless thing once in a while instead of every time. A skeleton screen so the user feels better about waiting for something that never needed to take that long.

I was optimizing the app instead of understanding it. And those are not the same activity — they're barely even related. One of them I could do fast, from memory, off a checklist, without ever opening the slow path and looking at it. The other one required me to actually sit down and find out what my own homepage was doing for eight seconds. Guess which one I did for a month first.

What it was actually doing

When I finally ran a trace instead of adding a feature — when I just watched, request by request, what the page did between "user hits enter" and "page appears" — the answer was almost funny.

To render the homepage — a greeting, a nav bar, and three little cards — the server was taking a guided tour of the entire database before it sent a single byte.

It loaded the user. Then, using something off the user, it loaded their organization. Then, using something off the organization, it loaded every project in that org. Then, for each project, one at a time, it loaded that project's most recent activity so it could maybe show a timestamp on a card the user would probably scroll right past. Each of those requests waited politely for the one before it to finish. A waterfall — one long single-file line of queries, each one blocking the next, the whole page holding its breath until the last straggler came back.

Eight seconds. To draw a greeting and three cards. The server wasn't slow. The database wasn't slow. The site was slow because it had decided, somewhere, years ago, that it couldn't render the top of the page until it had fetched the bottom of a data structure almost nobody looked at.

None of my optimizations touched this, because none of them could. A CDN can't parallelize a waterfall. A cache only helps the second visitor, and only if the data's the same, which it wasn't. Lazy-loading images does nothing for a page that's blocked on a chain of API calls before it paints at all. I'd been tuning the delivery of a payload the page should never have been waiting on in the first place.

The fix was understanding, not code

The actual change was small and boring, which is how you know it was the right one.

Render the shell immediately — the greeting, the nav, the cards' outlines — with the handful of things the first screen genuinely needs. Fetch those few things in parallel instead of in a chain. Everything else — the per-project activity, the stuff below the fold, the data for the card nobody clicks — load it after the page is already on the screen, or when someone actually asks for it.

That was it. The page went from eight seconds to about one. Not because I'd added a faster anything, but because I'd finally asked the question I'd spent a month avoiding: does this request need to happen before the user sees the page — does it need to happen at all? For most of that waterfall, the honest answer was no. It had just never occurred to anyone to ask, because adding the next fetch had always been easier than questioning the last one.

The code diff was tiny. The understanding behind it was the entire job.

The part that isn't free anymore

Here's the reframe, and it's the whole point.

Adding a fast thing is nearly free now. I can ask a machine to add a caching layer, wire up a CDN, memoize a component, lazy-load a route, and have plausible, working code back before my coffee's cool. So can you. The performance checklist — the whole catalogue of add-this-to-go-faster — has basically collapsed to a sentence and a few seconds of waiting. Adding speed, as an activity, has never been cheaper or more tireless.

But none of that is the same as knowing why your app is slow, and that part didn't get cheaper at all. Finding the eight-second waterfall meant holding the actual shape of the request graph in my head — what calls what, what waits on what, what the first screen truly needs versus what got loaded "just in case" by someone who's long gone. No tool handed me that. A tool will very happily add a sixth optimization on top of a problem it doesn't understand, because adding is exactly what it's good at. It will not, unprompted, tell you that the first five were treating a symptom.

You can't cache your way out of not understanding your own app.

The tools let me bolt on five optimizations in an afternoon. It took me a week to find the one request that was the whole problem — and that week, not the afternoon, was the actual engineering. Speed isn't something you add. Slowness is something you understand. The adding got free this year; the understanding didn't, and it never will.

To be clear — this is not "optimizations are bad"

I need to be fair here, because the lazy version of this post is "real engineers profile, juniors just add a CDN," and that's garbage.

I'm not anti-optimization. The CDN stayed. The caching stayed — it's genuinely useful now that the page isn't doing pointless work behind it. Lazy-loading, code-splitting, the skeleton screen: all still there, all still earning their keep. Adding fast things is good, and on a page that's already doing the right amount of work, that checklist is exactly how you squeeze out the last stretch. I'd add every one of them again.

The point is narrower, and I think more useful: adding speed was never the scarce part, so getting faster at adding it didn't make my site fast — it just let me pile optimizations on top of a problem I hadn't looked at. The scarce thing — the only thing that actually took eight seconds down to one — was the judgment to open the slow path and ask what work was even happening and whether it needed to. The tools made the adding free and did absolutely nothing about that question. They can't. They optimize confidently in whatever direction you point them — including straight onto the pile.

Why this is exactly how I build now

I build an agent platform now, and this one slow homepage is more or less the whole thesis of it.

The industry's reflex this year is to worship the author — the thing that generates. Look how much it ships! A caching layer from a sentence! But an author with no counterweight doesn't hand you a fast app. It hands you my homepage: five reasonable optimizations stacked confidently on top of a waterfall nobody questioned, because generating the next fast-thing was always easier than understanding the slow one underneath. I did it by hand for a month. The author is how the pile of fast things gets built.

So the part I care about isn't the author — I already assume the author. Everyone has one now. What I'm hunting for is the skeptic and the human. The author adds the optimization, fast and free. The skeptic is the part that asks the question I avoided for a month — does this request need to happen at all? what is the first screen actually waiting on? — and whose best output is often "delete four of these calls," not a sixth one. And the human is the one who owns the real person on the other end — someone on a phone on a train, watching a spinner for eight seconds, one thumb-twitch from gone. Author, skeptic, human. That separation is the entire shape of xenition — and it's the same thing one slow page taught me the hard way: generating the fast thing is free and always will be; knowing why it's slow, and what the person on the other end loses while they wait, is the whole job, and the only part anyone ever actually pays for.

My homepage didn't get fast when I ran out of optimizations to add. It got fast the afternoon I finally understood what it had been doing all along.

Next time your app is slow, don't reach for the checklist first. Open the slow path and watch what it actually does — and ask how much of that work was ever needed at all.

articles.title: Google Sheets is my favourite free backend
articles.description: I made a small game for my daughter. It's called Počítadlo ("counter" in Czech), and it's a simple...
articles.body_html:
I made a small game for my daughter. It's called Počítadlo ("counter" in Czech), and it's a simple counting game that helps her learn the basics of math: adding and subtracting up to 20, ten questions, a timer and a trophy when she beats her record. It runs as a PWA on her iPad.

After a few days I wanted to know how she actually uses it. How often does she play, which levels, how long does it take her, where does she make mistakes? And I wanted it as an email to me and my wife every evening, because nobody is going to open a dashboard.

The obvious answer is a database, an API and some email service. For a kids' game that's way too much. So I used a Google Sheet and Apps Script. It costs nothing, there's no server, and it took one evening, most of which was me fighting Google's settings.

In this post, I'll walk you through:

  • how the app sends data to a Google Sheet
  • how the Sheet sends a daily email
  • the gotchas that cost me most of that evening

The idea

Every Google Sheet can have an Apps Script attached to it (Extensions → Apps Script). Apps Script is just JavaScript running on Google's servers, and it can do two things that matter here:

  1. Be deployed as a web app: you get a URL, and doPost(e) runs every time someone POSTs to it.
  2. Run functions on a schedule and send email with MailApp.

So the Sheet is the database, the script is the API, and Gmail is the email service. All free.

Receiving data

The script side is tiny. Parse the JSON, append rows:

function doPost(e) {
  const events = JSON.parse(e.postData.contents);
  const sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActiveSpreadsheet().getSheetByName("events");
  const rows = events.map((ev) => [new Date(), new Date(ev.ts), ev.type, ev.level, ev.seconds, ev.mistakes]);
  sheet.getRange(sheet.getLastRow() + 1, 1, rows.length, rows[0].length).setValues(rows);
  return ContentService.createTextOutput("ok");
}

Then Deploy → New deployment → Web app, Execute as: Me, Who has access: Anyone. You get a URL ending with /exec.

In the app, I send events like "app opened", "level started", "level finished in 53 seconds with one mistake". The call looks like this:

await fetch(URL, {
  method: "POST",
  mode: "no-cors",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "text/plain" },
  body: JSON.stringify(events),
});

Two things here are important:

  • text/plain, not application/json. A JSON content type makes the browser send a CORS preflight, and Apps Script can't answer it. With text/plain there's no preflight, and you still JSON.parse it on the other side.
  • no-cors means you can't read the response. A resolved fetch only tells you the request reached Google. Not that the script worked. Keep that in mind, it bit me later.

The iPad is not always online, so events go to a queue in localStorage first and get sent when there's a connection. Nothing gets lost when she plays in the car.

Sending the email

The report is a normal function. It reads the rows, counts games, best and average times per level, and lists the wrong answers. Then:

MailApp.sendEmail({ to: EMAILS, name: "Počítadlo", subject, htmlBody: html });

The name matters more than you'd think. Without it the email comes "from you", Gmail files it under Sent, and you think it never arrived. Ask me how I know.

For the schedule, you create a trigger:

function setup() {
  ScriptApp.newTrigger("check").timeBased().everyMinutes(15).create();
}

check does nothing before 19:00. After that, it sends the report once and remembers the date in PropertiesService. Why not just a daily trigger at 19:00? Read on.

The gotchas

This is where my evening went.

The trigger doesn't exist until you run setup by hand. Obvious in hindsight. Pasting the code creates nothing. You have to pick setup in the function dropdown and press Run. My first evening email never came because there was no trigger at all.

"At 19:00" means "sometime between 19:00 and 20:00". Google runs time triggers at any minute inside the window. A 15-minute check that sends on its first run after 19:00 gets you within 15 minutes, and if one run fails, the next one catches up.

403 "access denied" with access set to Anyone. The web app returned Google Drive's "you need access" page to everyone, even though the settings were right. It went away after I ran a function in the editor and approved the permissions. The script had simply never been authorized.

"Sorry, unable to open the file at this time." That's Apps Script telling you that you're logged into more than one Google account. Use a private window with only the account that owns the Sheet.

New deployment vs. new version. Deploy → New deployment gives you a new URL. To update the code and keep the URL, go to Manage deployments → Edit → Version: New version. The scheduled functions always run the latest saved code, so changes to the email need only a save.

Make it tell you it's alive. Since no-cors hides everything, I added a doGet that lists the triggers and when the last report went out. Opening the URL in a browser shows me whether the schedule exists.

Your hosting will play your game. The same evening there were app opens with no games in them. It was Vercel, opening every new deploy in a headless browser to take a screenshot for the dashboard. Now everything not running as the installed app gets a web- prefix on its session ID, and the email skips those. I don't drop them, just mark them. If the detection is ever wrong on the iPad, I still have the data.

Limits

This is not a real backend and I wouldn't pretend it is.

  • The web app URL is in your JavaScript, so anyone can POST to it. Validate what comes in. Worst case for me is junk rows in a spreadsheet.
  • A free Gmail account can send 100 emails a day with MailApp. For one report a day, fine.
  • It's slow and has quotas. For a few hundred rows a day from one iPad, I'll never notice. For your startup, use a real database.

Was it worth it?

Yes. For something like this, it's perfect. The whole thing is one script file, a spreadsheet I can open on my phone, and an email at 19:00. I already know she gets stuck on 20 − 7, and that she beat her Level 1 record in her second game of the evening.

If you have a small personal project that needs to store a bit of data or send you a summary, try a Sheet before you spin up a server. The code is on GitHub in the tracking folder.

What's your favourite "free backend" hack? Drop a comment.

articles.title: Securing an Angular Firebase AI App with Email/Password Authentication (Part 2: Signal Forms Sign-In Modal) [GDE]
articles.description: In this blog post, we build a Sign-In modal component (SignInModalComponent) using the stable Angular...
articles.body_html:
In this blog post, we build a Sign-In modal component (SignInModalComponent) using the stable Angular Signal Forms API (@angular/forms/signals) to handle email and password authentication.


Caption: Sign-In Dialog with email and password fields.

Architecture & Mental Model

The sign-in flow works as follows:

  • Signal Form Validation: We build a Signal Form with required email and password fields. When validation fails on submit, onInvalid automatically focuses the first invalid control.
  • Firebase Authentication: When a user submits valid form fields, SignInModalComponent calls AuthService.signIn() to verify that the submitted email and password match an existing account in Firebase Authentication.
  • Route Redirection or Error Handling:
    • Valid credentials: When authentication succeeds (AuthService.isAuthenticated() is true), the modal closes and redirects the user to the /dashboard route, where they can perform AI tasks.
    • Invalid credentials / error thrown: When authentication fails, SignInModalComponent.signIn() updates its errorMessage signal ('Failed to sign in. Please check your credentials and try again.') and returns { kind: 'serverError', message: 'Failed to submit form' }. 
flowchart TD
    Submit["User Submits Email & Password"] --> Validate{"signInSchemaValidation()"}
    Validate -- "Invalid" --> Focus["onInvalid: focusBoundControl() on 1st error"]
    Validate -- "Valid" --> Action["submission.action: signIn(field)"]
    Action --> Auth["AuthService.signIn(formValues)"]
    Auth --> Check{"AuthService.isAuthenticated()?"}
    Check -- "true" --> Close["DialogRef.close() + Router.navigate(['/dashboard'])"]
    Check -- "false / throws" --> Error["Set errorMessage signal & return serverError"]

1. Defining the Signal Form Validation Schema

We start by importing the required and email validators from @angular/forms/signals to define signInSchemaValidation(), which returns a SchemaOrSchemaFn<AuthCredentials, PathKind.Root>:

  • Required fields (required): The required validator marks both the email and password fields as required with custom error messages ({ message: 'Email is required' } and { message: 'Password is required' }).
  • Email format validation (email): The email validator checks that the entered email value is a well-formed email address and returns { message: 'Invalid email format' } when the format is invalid. 
// src/app/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/schemas/sign-in.schema.ts
import type { AuthCredentials } from '@/core/auth';
import type { PathKind, SchemaOrSchemaFn } from '@angular/forms/signals';
import { email, required } from '@angular/forms/signals';

export function signInSchemaValidation(): SchemaOrSchemaFn<AuthCredentials, PathKind.Root> {
  return (schemaPath) => {
    required(schemaPath.email, { message: 'Email is required' });
    email(schemaPath.email, { message: 'Invalid email format' });
    required(schemaPath.password, { message: 'Password is required' });
  };
}

2. Building SignInModalComponent with Signal Forms and AuthService

2.1 Injecting Dependencies and Initializing the Signal Form

In SignInModalComponent, we inject the required services and initialize the reactive form model:

  • AuthService and Router: Handle Firebase email/password authentication and route navigation after signing in.
  • DialogRef: Closes the modal via @angular/cdk/dialog (inject(DialogRef, { optional: true })) when the user clicks the close button or when sign-in succeeds.
  • errorMessage: Stores and displays an alert message (signal<string | undefined>(undefined)) when authentication fails.
  • signInModel: Backs the Signal Form (signal<AuthCredentials>({ email: '', password: '' })) and initializes the email and password fields to empty strings.

Note

Why @angular/cdk/dialog instead of a native <dialog> element?
If you only need a single modal in an app without @angular/cdk, the native HTML <dialog> element is the better, zero-dependency choice. However, this repository already includes @angular/cdk, and @angular/cdk/dialog provides comprehensive accessibility (a11y) out of the box—including focus trapping, focus restoration, Escape-key dismissal, and ARIA attributes. Because we also dynamically import @angular/cdk/dialog when opening the modal, so it never increases the initial bundle size, it is a practical choice here.

// src/app/core/auth/auth-credentials.interface.ts
export interface AuthCredentials {
  email: string;
  password: string;
}

// src/app/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component.ts (Part 1a: Dependencies & Model)
@Component({
  imports: [FormField, FormRoot, CloseIconComponent, SpinnerIconComponent],
  selector: 'app-sign-in-modal',
})
export class SignInModalComponent {
  readonly #authService = inject(AuthService);
  readonly #dialogRef = inject(DialogRef, { optional: true });
  readonly #router = inject(Router);

  errorMessage = signal<string | undefined>(undefined);

  signInModel = signal<AuthCredentials>({
    email: '',
    password: '',
  });

Next, we pass this.signInModel and signInSchemaValidation() to the form() function to create signInForm. The form() function validates signInModel against the validation schema and configures form submission behavior:

  • Valid submission (submission.action): When validation succeeds, form submission executes the action callback, which invokes this.signIn(field).
  • Invalid submission (submission.onInvalid): When validation fails, form submission executes the onInvalid callback to locate the first validation error (field().errorSummary()[0]) and automatically focus its bound form control (firstError?.fieldTree().focusBoundControl()). 
// src/app/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component.ts (Part 1b: Signal Form)
  signInForm = form(this.signInModel, signInSchemaValidation(), {
    submission: {
      action: async (field) => this.signIn(field),
      onInvalid: (field) => {
        const firstError = field().errorSummary()[0];
        firstError?.fieldTree().focusBoundControl();
      },
    },
  });

2.2 Implementing onClose() and signIn()

Next, let's implement the onClose() and signIn() methods in SignInModalComponent:

  • onClose(): Calls this.#dialogRef?.close() when the user clicks the top-right close button to dismiss the modal.
  • signIn(): Calls this.#authService.signIn(field().value()) to authenticate the submitted form credentials with Firebase Authentication:
    • Successful authentication: When this.#authService.isAuthenticated() evaluates to true, we close the modal (this.#dialogRef?.close()), navigate to the /dashboard route (await this.#router.navigate([APP_LINKS.DASHBOARD])), and return undefined.
    • Unsuccessful authentication: When authentication fails, we update this.errorMessage.set('Failed to sign in. Please check your credentials and try again.') and return a generic submission error ({ kind: 'serverError', message: 'Failed to submit form' }) so the Signal Form records the failed submission state. 
// src/app/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component.ts (Part 2: onClose & signIn)
  onClose(): void {
    this.#dialogRef?.close();
  }

  async signIn(field: FieldTree<AuthCredentials, string | number>): Promise<SignInSubmissionError | undefined> {
    this.errorMessage.set(undefined);
    await this.#authService.signIn(field().value());
    if (this.#authService.isAuthenticated()) {
      this.#dialogRef?.close();
      await this.#router.navigate([APP_LINKS.DASHBOARD]);
      return undefined;
    }
    this.errorMessage.set('Failed to sign in. Please check your credentials and try again.');
    return { kind: 'serverError', message: 'Failed to submit form' };
  }
}

3. Binding the Signal Form in the Template

Now let's wire signInForm to the component template in src/app/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component.html:

  • Closing the modal: When a user clicks the top-right close button, onClose() closes the modal via this.#dialogRef?.close().
  • Displaying authentication errors: When errorMessage() holds a message (@if (errorMessage(); as msg)), the template renders <div role="alert">{{ msg }}</div> above the form.
  • Binding the form root ([formRoot]): The [formRoot] directive binds the <form> element directly to the signInForm form model, connecting form submission to the submission configuration we defined in the component.
  • Binding form fields ([formField]): The [formField] directive binds signInForm.email to the email input field and signInForm.password to the password input field.
  • Rendering validation errors: When the user interacts with a field (touched()) and it is invalid(), we iterate over its errors() array with @for to output each validation error message ({{ error.message }}).
  • Handling the submission state: While the form's async submission.action is running, signInForm().submitting() evaluates to true. We bind [disabled]="signInForm().submitting()" on the submit button to disable it during authentication and prevent concurrent submissions. 
<!-- src/app/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component.html (Signal Form excerpt) -->
@if (errorMessage(); as msg) {
