What's this blog about?

I'm learning full-stack development (React, Node, MongoDB) alongside AI/ML, and I'm documenting all of it here. Not the polished highlight reel. The real stuff: what I built, what broke, and what finally fixed it.

What to expect

  • 🛠️ Project breakdowns: how I built things, and why I made the choices I did
  • 🐛 Bug diaries: the errors that ate my evenings, and the one-line fixes that ended them
  • 🤖 AI/ML experiments: small, honest explorations, no hype
  • 📚 Learning notes: resources and roadmaps that actually helped

A tiny tip to start

Stop debugging with plain console.log. When you're dealing with arrays of objects, try this:

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "A", active: true },
  { id: 2, name: "B", active: false },
];

console.table(users);

You get a clean, readable table in the console instead of a wall of nested objects. Small change, huge sanity saver.

Why write in public?

Because explaining something is the fastest way to find out whether I really understand it. And if even one person reads a post and thinks "oh, I'm not the only one stuck on this," it's worth it.

Let's connect

If you're also learning, building, or just here for the error messages, drop a comment: what's the first project you ever built? I'd love to hear it.

See you in the next post. Until then, may your builds be green and your errors be descriptive. 🟢

articles.title: Rack Before You Remember
articles.description: What racking wine teaches about agent memory    The mead's lees on October 21, with the racking cane...
articles.body_html:
What racking wine teaches about agent memory

The mead's lees on October 21, with the racking cane at the edge. Everything the siphon left behind stays here.

That layer at the bottom of my mead fermenter did most of the work of turning honey and water into something worth drinking. It's spent yeast and the debris of a few weeks of vigorous fermentation. Without it, there'd be nothing to rack.

I left all of it behind on purpose.

What lees are, and why they stay behind

When primary fermentation winds down, the yeast that did the work drops out of suspension along with whatever solids came along for the ride. That sediment is called the lees, and the first, heaviest layer is known as the gross lees.

Racking is how you separate the wine from it. You siphon the wine off from above, carefully, into a clean vessel, and leave the sediment where it settled. I racked the pear wine on October 12, once the readings had held steady long enough to justify the move, and the mead on October 21, when its refractometer reading had settled at 3.2 Brix.

The pear racking went smoothly, and it taught me something I didn't expect. I'd added bentonite, a clay that binds proteins and helps haze drop out, and I assumed that by racking day the wine would be close to see-through. It wasn't. It's not murky, but it's not clear either. Racking had separated the wine from the heavy sediment. It hadn't made the wine clean. The finer material still in suspension will take weeks to settle, and there will be another racking after it does.

Hold on to that distinction, because it comes back later.

The reason to rack isn't that the lees are bad. It's that their job is done. Left in contact with the wine too long, the heavy lees start to break down, and the compounds they release can push the wine toward off flavors that range from dull to genuinely unpleasant. Material that was essential during fermentation becomes a liability during aging.

That's the whole article in one sentence: not everything useful during execution deserves to survive execution.

Agents have lees too

Watch an AI agent work through a nontrivial task and you'll see the equivalent of a primary fermentation. It retrieves documents, most of which turn out to be irrelevant. It calls tools and gets back large blobs of output. It tries an approach, hits an error, and backs out. It forms hypotheses that don't survive. It reads text from untrusted sources, some of which might contain instructions it was never supposed to follow.

All of that is essential while the task is running. The failed attempts are how it found the working one. The irrelevant documents are how it figured out which were relevant.

And then the task ends, and a surprising number of memory designs do the equivalent of never racking the wine. The transcript gets saved. The tool outputs get embedded. The scratchpad gets summarized into long-term memory without anyone deciding which parts of it were conclusions and which were sediment.

For a while, nothing seems wrong. Then the lees start to break down. A hypothesis the agent abandoned on Tuesday gets retrieved on Friday as if it were a fact. An error message from a transient outage becomes a durable belief that some service is broken. A snippet of injected text from a web page resurfaces, weeks later, in a context where it looks like a user preference. None of these were bad things to have during the task. They're bad things to have in the cellar.

You can't filter it out at the glass

The obvious objection is that you can sort it out later. Store everything, and let retrieval figure out what's relevant.

Winemaking has a pretty clear answer to that. If you leave the wine on the gross lees for months, you can't fix it by pouring carefully. The problem isn't that sediment ends up in the glass; you could decant that away. The problem is what the sediment did to the wine while it was stored together.

Memory systems work the same way. Raw execution material doesn't just sit inertly waiting to be filtered at read time. It gets summarized, and the summaries inherit its errors. It gets embedded, and it competes in similarity search with things that were actually true. It feeds derived facts, and those facts get cited by later tasks. By the time a read-side filter sees it, the contamination has already been folded into things that look clean.

None of this means throwing the raw record away. Transcripts and tool outputs are genuinely valuable for debugging, forensics, and compliance, and a system that can't reconstruct what an agent did is its own kind of problem. The distinction is between keeping evidence and promoting it into memory. A raw execution log in an archive the agent never retrieves from is evidence. The same log embedded into the store the agent reasons from is sediment in the wine. Winemakers make the same split: lees you want to keep go into a separate jar, for cooking or for starting the next batch. They don't stay in the carboy.

That's why I've come to think the decision about what persists belongs at write time, as a deliberate boundary, rather than being deferred to whatever happens to read the store later. I've been calling this Write-Side Custody: the system that writes memory is responsible for what it lets in, and for being able to say why.

One boundary doesn't make it clean

Remember the hazy pear. A write-time boundary works the same way the first racking does: it removes the gross sediment, the material that's obviously done its job and is obviously going to cause trouble. It doesn't guarantee that what passes through is perfectly clean.

Some fine material always comes along. A conclusion that seemed confirmed turns out to rest on a shaky source. A summary carries a little of the noise it was built from. That isn't a reason to skip the boundary. It's a reason to expect more than one. Wine gets racked again after it has had time to settle, because time reveals what the first separation couldn't. My blackberry wine got its second racking the same week as the mead's first, and weeks after the heavy sediment was gone, it still left a layer of fine lees behind. Memory benefits from the same second pass: revisiting what was stored once it has been used, contradicted, or simply aged, and deciding again what still deserves to stay.

The first racking makes the problem manageable. It doesn't make it finished.

The racking cane leaves wine behind

Here's the part nobody mentions in the metaphor-friendly version of racking: you lose wine.

To avoid drawing up sediment, you stop siphoning a little before the bottom, which means leaving some perfectly good wine behind with the lees. In a five-gallon batch that loss barely registers. In a one-gallon batch, it's noticeable.

The blackberry's second racking. The receiving carboy sits lower so gravity does the work.

The pear got lucky. I'd made a little more than the carboy could hold, so the loss came out of the surplus, and the surplus was just enough for one hydrometer reading. The mead lost four ounces to its lees, about 3% of the batch. The blackberry's second racking lost eight, about 6%, and not all of that was sediment: the auto-siphon simply couldn't reach into the corners of the carboy. The shape of the vessel set part of the cost.

A carboy that isn't full has headspace, and headspace is air, and air is how wine oxidizes. So the gap has to be filled with something. For the mead, I topped it back up with four ounces of honey water, made from the same fireweed honey, at 18.4 Brix, which means the mead now has a little fresh sugar in it, on purpose, and the log says so. For the blackberry, I didn't have anything worth adding, so I used an inert gas instead. It doesn't replace the missing wine. The carboy holds less than it did, and nothing will change that. What the gas does is protect the wine that's left, by keeping oxygen away from it.

That's an honest cost, and it's the right trade. Chasing the last few ounces means stirring up the sediment you were trying to leave behind.

Memory boundaries have the same cost. A write-side filter conservative enough to keep out the sediment will sometimes discard something that would have been useful: a detail from a failed attempt, a tool output that mattered after all. That's not a flaw in the approach. It's the price of the boundary, and it's usually far cheaper than the alternative. A memory store that has lost a few useful details is annoying. One that has absorbed a few confidently wrong ones is dangerous, because it doesn't know which ones they are.

It's worth separating the two kinds of loss, though, because the blackberry had both. Some of what stayed behind was sediment I chose to leave. The rest was wine the siphon physically couldn't reach. Memory systems lose information the same two ways. Some is discarded by policy: a rule decided this didn't deserve to persist. Some is lost to the equipment: a schema with no field for it, a fixed chunk size that splits it in half, a context limit that drops whatever came first. Nobody decided to lose that second kind, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed. The fixes are different, too. A bad policy gets a better rule. A bad vessel gets better equipment, and no amount of careful siphoning will reach a corner the tube can't bend into.

And when the boundary leaves a gap, those two top-offs are worth remembering. Adding something real is fine when it's deliberate and recorded: the mead's top-off is a known liquid at a known strength, written down the day it went in. The trouble is filling the space with something that only looks like the real thing: a plausible guess, a synthesized summary, a default. That's topping up with water and not mentioning it. It dilutes the record, and nobody can tell afterward which part was the wine. When there's nothing real to add, do what the inert gas does. A record that says plainly this was discarded, and here's why doesn't restore what was lost. It protects everything downstream from treating the gap as something known. That's the job: not filling the hole, but making sure nothing mistakes the hole for knowledge.

Sur lie is a decision

To be fair to the lees, some winemakers deliberately keep wine on them. Aging on the fine lees, the lighter sediment that remains after the first racking, is a traditional technique for adding texture and complexity. It's called sur lie, and Muscadet and Champagne are built partly on it.

But notice how it's done. It's the fine lees, not the gross lees. It's a specific choice made for a specific wine, often with regular stirring and attention. Nobody ends up with a sur lie wine because they forgot to rack.

The same is true in memory. Sometimes execution detail genuinely deserves to persist. A failed approach might be exactly the thing you want an agent to remember next time: we tried this, it doesn't work, here's why. That's valuable. But it's valuable because someone decided to keep it, labeled it as what it is, and recorded where it came from. A lesson learned from a failure is a different thing from the failure's raw transcript sitting in the store, waiting to be mistaken for advice.

Keeping execution material can be the right call. Keeping it by default almost never is.

Rack at transitions, not constantly

One more practical lesson. Racking isn't free for the wine either: every transfer exposes it to oxygen and handling. So you don't rack constantly. You rack at transitions, when primary ends, after secondary, before bottling, at the points where the evidence says the wine has moved into a new state. The mead waited in primary until its readings held still, then moved once.

That maps well onto memory design. Rather than continuously streaming everything an agent touches into durable storage, the natural points to decide what persists are the transitions: when a task completes, when a conclusion is confirmed, when a session ends. Those are the moments when you can tell the wine from the sediment, because the process has finished producing both.

Racking your memory

Decide what persists at write time. Read-time filtering can't undo what raw material did to summaries, embeddings, and derived facts while it sat in the store.

Archive evidence; don't promote it. Keep raw transcripts for debugging and audit, somewhere the agent doesn't retrieve from. Evidence and memory are different stores.

Assume execution produces sediment. Failed attempts, irrelevant retrievals, transient errors, and untrusted text are normal byproducts of useful work. Plan for them to exist; don't plan for them to persist.

Expect more than one pass. The first boundary removes the obvious sediment. Time reveals the rest.

Accept the cost of the boundary. A good filter will occasionally discard something useful. That's cheaper than keeping something wrong.

Know which losses are policy and which are equipment. Some information is dropped because a rule said so. Some is dropped because the schema, chunk size, or context limit couldn't hold it. Only the first kind was a decision.

Fill gaps honestly. When the boundary leaves a hole, either add something real and record exactly what it was, or record that something was removed, so the gap is protected rather than mistaken for knowledge. Never top it up with plausible filler.

Make retention deliberate. When execution detail is worth keeping, keep it on purpose, label what it is, and record where it came from.

Rack at transitions. The best time to separate conclusions from sediment is when the process that produced them has finished.

The pear is clearing now, a few shades brighter than it was in the fermenter, though still not as clear as I'd hoped. The lees did their job. They just don't get to come along for the rest of it.

articles.title: Why 80% on OSWorld Required VM Snapshot Rollbacks
articles.description: If you have ever watched an autonomous computer-use agent work through a desktop operating system,...
articles.body_html:
If you have ever watched an autonomous computer-use agent work through a desktop operating system, you know the exact moment the rollout dies.

The agent handles the first eight steps cleanly. It launches the browser, navigates to the admin panel, and exports a CSV report. Then, on step nine, it misclicks a dropdown menu, clicks the desktop background to recover, and accidentally dismisses the modal.

From that single mistake, the environment state is corrupted. On step ten, the file the agent expects to inspect does not exist. On step eleven, the agent begins rationalizing why the window looks different. By step fifteen, it is typing random terminal commands into an unfocused window, burning tokens on a trajectory that was doomed five minutes ago.

Every engineering team training computer-use models runs straight into this wall. The standard reaction is to treat the environment like a disposable container: throw the entire virtual machine away, spin up a fresh image, and start the rollout over from step one.

A paper from researchers at MMLab CUHK, Tsinghua University, HKUST(GZ), and JD Explore Academy, titled CUA-Master, takes a different path. Their 27-billion-parameter model, CUA-Master-27B, achieved a score of 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, alongside 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0 and 43.9 on WeaveBench.

The performance did not come from an enormous model or thousands of hours of synthetic self-play. It came from treating operating system interaction like a transactional runtime with snapshot rollbacks.

The cost of throwing away the sandbox

To train a policy that can navigate desktop applications, you need tens of thousands of verified execution trajectories. But real operating systems are stateful and unforgiving.

When a multi-step rollout fails, discarding the entire run creates two problems.

First, it destroys valid compute. If an agent executes thirteen correct actions and stumbles on the fourteenth, tossing the run discards thirteen high-quality demonstration steps. The infrastructure has to reboot the VM, reinstall dependencies, restore seed data, and wait for the model to reproduce the identical prefix.

Second, the alternative is worse. If you do not discard the run and instead let the model attempt recovery, the model frequently generates noisy, self-contradicting actions. If those corrupted suffixes enter your training dataset, the policy learns to hallucinate around broken state instead of executing clean workflows.

CUA-Master solves this with a mechanism called Resilient Trajectory Collection.

Snapshot rollback as a branching search

Instead of restarting from scratch when a task fails or shows operational inefficiency, the CUA-Master runtime uses incremental virtual machine snapshots.

As the agent works, the environment infrastructure creates lightweight snapshots at stable operational boundaries. Each snapshot records the full memory state of the virtual machine alongside a structured signature: active window handles, layout geometry, open file descriptors, and controller metadata.

When the environment verifier flags a failure, a dedicated detector examines three artifacts together: the verifier residuals, the executed trajectory, and the final environment state.

From that comparison, the detector calculates the earliest step where the agent diverged from the intended task state. It also produces execution-grounded diagnostic feedback explaining what went wrong, such as an unhandled modal or a missing target directory, without leaking privileged action labels that would cause distribution mismatch during training.

Once the divergence step is identified, the runtime does not reset the VM to the beginning. It rolls the virtual machine back to the latest snapshot taken immediately before that step.

The policy engine keeps the successful prefix, drops the failed suffix, and resumes execution from the restored state, using the diagnostic feedback as a local hint.

The agent branches outward from the point of failure until the verifier confirms success or exhausts a retry budget. When the run finishes, only the cleanest, shortest passing branch is kept for supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Every failed or redundant branch is discarded.

This changes data collection from an all-or-nothing lottery into a localized graph search. The training pipeline collects valid, high-efficiency trajectories while reusing the expensive prefixes that already succeeded.

Mining real video tutorials instead of hallucinating tasks

The second bottleneck in computer-use agents is task diversity.

If you prompt an LLM to generate synthetic desktop tasks, it invents toy problems. It asks to rename three text files in a folder or calculate a sum in a spreadsheet. Those synthetic setups lack the friction of real desktop software, which involves nested menus, modal dialogs, sluggish network tabs, and arbitrary OS quirks.

CUA-Master bootstraps its task pool through open-world seeding. The researchers harvested video tutorials from platforms like YouTube and TikTok.

A raw instructional video cannot be used directly as an agent prompt. Tutorials contain conversational intros, sponsored segments, and non-actionable chatter. The CUA-Master pipeline uses multimodal temporal episode discovery to slice tutorials into discrete software tasks.

From each clip, a dual-path reconstruction pipeline pairs semantic transcript analysis with visual keyframe tracking. It reconstructs the sequence of actions that the human demonstrator executed, verifies them against local application state, and extracts atomic action primitives.

Those primitives then feed an autocatalytic propagation pipeline. The system recombines verified primitives into composable, multi-application workflows that come with executable verification scripts. Instead of training on synthetic guesses, the model trains on composable variations of authentic human software use.

Blending terminal commands with GUI clicks

The third structural design in the framework is a unified hybrid action space.

Pure visual computer-use agents try to solve every problem through the graphical interface. If an agent needs to find a string across fifty files, it opens a file manager, clicks into each folder, and opens text editors one by one. That approach burns dozens of visual inference steps, introduces dozens of opportunities for misclicks, and runs orders of magnitude slower than a simple shell command.

CLI-only agents have the opposite problem: they fail the moment an operation requires interacting with proprietary desktop software, visual canvases, or browser authentications that lack an API.

CUA-Master gives the agent access to both direct GUI primitives (mouse clicks, scrolling, keystrokes) and structured CLI execution (shell.exec). If a task involves searching logs, moving directories, or checking process tables, the agent runs shell commands. When the workflow moves into GIMP, LibreOffice, or Chrome, the agent switches to mouse and keyboard controls.

In ablation benchmarks across hybrid tasks, this dual-interface setup delivered substantial performance and latency improvements over GUI-only baselines.

What builders should take from this

The headline number from the paper is 80.2 on OSWorld Verified for a 27B model, which puts it within striking distance of proprietary frontier models like Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.

The takeaway for engineers building agent systems is about runtime architecture.

If you want reliable agents in complex environments, you cannot treat execution as an uninterrupted straight line. Long-horizon automation requires the harness to manage state boundaries. When an agent inevitably missteps in an OS sandbox, rolling back to a clean checkpoint and retrying the divergence step is far cheaper than rebooting the world or hoping the model talks its way out of trouble.

articles.title: Are You a Python Developer or a Python Expert? 8 Tests I Failed Hijacking Win+Shift+S in One 7,600-Line File
articles.description: Most Python developers can parse a CSV, write a decorator and pip install their way out of a...
articles.body_html:
Most Python developers can parse a CSV, write a decorator and pip install their way out of a problem.

Python experts know what happens when the operating system doesn't want you to do the thing: when a hotkey is reserved, when an audio device goes quiet, when a screen grab is slower than your frame rate, and when ctypes quietly cuts your pointers in half.

I found out which one I was while building ASNIPP: a screenshot tool, screen recorder, live-drawing overlay, colour picker and video editor for Windows. It is one Python file, about 7,600 lines, with no ads, no analytics and no network calls. Everything runs on your machine.

Every test below is a real bug or design decision from that file. The code is trimmed for reading, but the ideas are exactly what ships. Score yourself honestly. 👇

Test 1: Can you take a hotkey that Windows says is reserved?

I wanted Win+Shift+S to open ASNIPP instead of the Snipping Tool. The obvious tool is RegisterHotKey. It fails: that combo belongs to the shell.

The way in is a low-level keyboard hook (WH_KEYBOARD_LL) through ctypes. It sees the keystroke before anyone else, and if your callback returns 1, the key never reaches Windows.

def cb(nCode, wParam, lParam):
    if nCode == 0 and wParam in (0x100, 0x101, 0x104, 0x105):   # key down / up
        kb = ctypes.cast(lParam, ctypes.POINTER(_KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT)).contents
        if kb.vkCode in SNIP_HOOK_KEYS:                         # only S and R, nothing else
            action, self._pending[kb.vkCode] = snip_hook_decision(
                kb.vkCode, wParam in (0x100, 0x104), bool(kb.flags & 0x10),
                pressed(0x5B, 0x5C), pressed(0x10), pressed(0x11), pressed(0x12),
                self._pending.get(kb.vkCode, False))
            if action == "trigger":
                u.keybd_event(0xE8, 0, 0, 0)    # inject an unassigned key...
                u.keybd_event(0xE8, 0, 2, 0)    # ...so releasing Win doesn't open Start
                QTimer.singleShot(0, lambda: self.on_trigger("photo"))
                return 1                        # swallowed
            if action == "swallow":
                return 1
    return u.CallNextHookEx(None, nCode, wParam, lParam)

self._proc = HOOKPROC(cb)    # keep a reference or it gets garbage-collected
self.hook = u.SetWindowsHookExW(13, self._proc, k.GetModuleHandleW(None), 0)

Four details separate "it works once" from "it works":

  1. Swallow the key-up too. If you eat the S press but let the release through, apps see a stray key-up. ASNIPP remembers it ate the press and eats exactly one release.
  2. Inject a dummy key (0xE8). Press and release Win alone and Windows opens Start. A harmless unassigned keystroke in between cancels that.
  3. Ignore injected events (flags & 0x10), or your own keybd_event call will trigger you again.
  4. The decision logic is a pure function with no ctypes in it, so it can be tested without a keyboard: 
def snip_hook_decision(vk, down, injected, win, shift, ctrl, alt, pending_up):
    if injected or vk not in SNIP_HOOK_KEYS:
        return "pass", pending_up
    if down:
        if win and shift and not ctrl and not alt:
            return "trigger", True
        return "pass", pending_up
    if pending_up:
        return "swallow", False
    return "pass", pending_up

It only looks at S and R while Win+Shift are held. Nothing is logged or stored, and the source says so at the top of the class, because a keyboard hook should always be honest about what it reads.

Developer: pip install keyboard.
Expert: knows where the hook sits in the input chain, and writes the state machine as a pure function.

Test 2: Why is my recording's audio 40 seconds shorter than the video?

ASNIPP records system audio with WASAPI loopback. The first test recording looked fine, until I played a video with long silent parts: the sound drifted further and further ahead of the picture.

The cause: loopback delivers no data at all while nothing is playing. No callbacks, no zeros, nothing. If you just append whatever arrives, silence disappears from the file and everything after it slides earlier.

The fix is to treat the wall clock as the truth and pad the gaps yourself:

def push(self, data):                      # called from the audio thread
    with self.lock:
        if self.fill:                      # only for loopback, not the mic
            now = rec.active_time()        # seconds of *unpaused* recording
            gap = int((now - n / self.rate) * self.rate) - self.frames
            if gap > self.rate * 0.12:     # ignore jitter under 120 ms
                self._zeros(gap)           # write real silence
        self.f.write(pcm.tobytes())
        self.frames += n

active_time() is perf_counter() minus the start time minus every second spent paused. So pausing the recording pauses the audio clock too.

Bonus trap: sounddevice has no WASAPI loopback. System audio needs PyAudioWPatch, with a "Stereo Mix" device as the fallback. ASNIPP tries both and tells the user which one is missing instead of silently recording nothing.

Developer: appends the bytes it receives.
Expert: asks "what does this API do when there is nothing to say?"

Test 3: What happens when grab() can't keep up with 30 FPS?

The recorder is a loop of mss.grab() → cv2.VideoWriter.write(). On a busy 4K screen a grab can take longer than 33 ms. If you write one frame per grab, a 10-second recording is stored as 6 seconds of video, and it plays back too fast.

The loop doesn't count frames. It counts time, and writes as many frames as the clock says are owed:

active += dt                                    # unpaused seconds so far
img = sct.grab(self.monitor)
fr = np.ascontiguousarray(np.asarray(img)[:, :, :3])   # BGRA -> BGR

target = int(active * fps) + 1                  # frames that SHOULD exist by now
n = max(1, min(target - written, fps))          # catch up, but never more than 1 s at once
for _ in range(n):
    out.write(fr)
written += n

wait = written / fps - (active + (time.perf_counter() - last))
if wait > 0:
    time.sleep(min(wait, 0.05))                 # too fast? sleep. Too slow? duplicate.

A slow machine gets a few repeated frames. A fast machine gets a sleep. Either way the video is exactly as long as the real recording, which is what keeps the audio from Test 2 in sync.

Two small things make it production-grade: the min(..., fps) cap stops a long stall from dumping thousands of frames, and the audio clock starts from an on_ready callback fired right before the first frame, so both streams share the same zero.

Developer: time.sleep(1/30) in a loop.
Expert: knows sleep is a request, not a guarantee, and schedules against a clock.

Test 4: Why did my mic get quieter when I turned on system audio?

After recording, ASNIPP mixes the system track and the mic track into the MP4 with ffmpeg. Turn on both and the voice sounded half as loud.

amix divides each input by the number of inputs by default. Two tracks, so each is halved. The fix is normalize=0, but not every ffmpeg build knows that option, so the mixer tries variants in order and moves on when one fails:

variants = [
    chains + [f"[a0][a1]amix=inputs=2:duration=longest:normalize=0,apad,atrim=0:{d}[m]"],
    chains + [f"[a0][a1]amix=inputs=2:duration=longest,volume=2,apad,atrim=0:{d}[m]"],  # older builds
]
for fc in variants:
    ok, err = run_ffmpeg(args + ["-filter_complex", ";".join(fc), ...])
    if ok:
        break

Look at the tail too: apad,atrim=0:{d}. If the audio is a hair shorter than the video, ffmpeg's -shortest would cut the video. Padding the audio and then trimming to the exact video length means a short track can never shorten the video.

And if ffmpeg is missing entirely? ASNIPP mixes the tracks in pure NumPy and saves a .wav next to the video, with a note saying what to install. It degrades, it doesn't crash.

Developer: ffmpeg -i a -i b out.mp4.
Expert: reads what each filter assumes, and keeps a plan B.

Test 5: Why does GetWindowLongPtrW return garbage in Python?

Live drawing mode puts a transparent overlay over your whole screen. Sometimes you want to click through it to the app underneath. That is the WS_EX_TRANSPARENT window style, set through ctypes:

u = ctypes.windll.user32
get_l, set_l = u.GetWindowLongPtrW, u.SetWindowLongPtrW

get_l.restype  = ctypes.c_ssize_t                       # <- the whole point
get_l.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_int]
set_l.restype  = ctypes.c_ssize_t
set_l.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_ssize_t]

hwnd = int(widget.winId())
st = get_l(hwnd, -20)                                    # GWL_EXSTYLE
st = (st | 0x20 | 0x80000) if on else (st & ~0x20)       # TRANSPARENT | LAYERED
set_l(hwnd, -20, st)

ctypes assumes every foreign function returns a 32-bit int and takes 32-bit arguments. On 64-bit Windows, handles and pointer-sized values are 64 bits, so without restype and argtypes you get truncated values, sign errors and crashes that only appear on some machines. Declare every signature, every time.

The function also falls back to Qt's own WA_TransparentForMouseEvents if the Win32 route fails, and a 32-bit Python gets GetWindowLongW instead. Same idea as Test 4: the ideal path first, and an honest fallback after.

Developer: copies the snippet from Stack Overflow.
Expert: writes down the C signature before calling the C function.

Test 6: Does "delete" actually mean delete?

ASNIPP's library has a delete button. os.remove() is permanent, and nobody forgives a tool that permanently deletes their screenshot after one misclick. So deleting sends the file to the Recycle Bin, using SHFileOperationW and no third-party package:

class SHFILEOPSTRUCTW(ctypes.Structure):
    _pack_ = 1 if ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_void_p) == 4 else 8     # 32 vs 64-bit layout
    _fields_ = [("hwnd", wt.HWND), ("wFunc", wt.UINT), ("pFrom", wt.LPCWSTR),
                ("pTo", wt.LPCWSTR), ("fFlags", ctypes.c_ushort),
                ("fAnyOperationsAborted", wt.BOOL), ("hNameMappings", ctypes.c_void_p),
                ("lpszProgressTitle", wt.LPCWSTR)]

op = SHFILEOPSTRUCTW()
op.wFunc = 3                                       # FO_DELETE
op.pFrom = os.path.abspath(path) + "\0"            # must end in TWO nulls (Python adds one)
op.fFlags = 0x40 | 0x10 | 0x4 | 0x400              # ALLOWUNDO | NOCONFIRM | SILENT | NOERRORUI
res = ctypes.windll.shell32.SHFileOperationW(ctypes.byref(op))
return res == 0 and not op.fAnyOperationsAborted and not os.path.exists(path)

The last line matters most. The function returns True only if the file is really gone. Not "the call returned 0". Not "no exception". The API said yes and the filesystem agrees.

If it can't reach the Recycle Bin (some network drives), the UI can say so rather than claim a delete that didn't happen.

Developer: trusts the return code.
Expert: verifies the world changed.

Test 7: Is your eyedropper accurate to the pixel on a scaled display?

ASNIPP has a colour picker with a magnifier and a pixel ruler. The first version was off by one pixel on my laptop, and by several on my friend's 150% display.

Two decisions fixed it:

1. Freeze the screen first. The picker doesn't read live pixels. It hides ASNIPP's own island, waits 160 ms for the compositor, grabs the screen once, and works on that frozen image. Menus, tooltips and hover states stay exactly as they were when you pressed the key.

def _grab_prepare(self, mode):
    self.island.hide()
    QTimer.singleShot(160, lambda: self._grab(mode))   # let the window really disappear

def _grab(self, mode):
    pix = screen.grabWindow(0)
    pix.setDevicePixelRatio(1.0)                        # work in true device pixels

2. Never assume widget size equals image size. Convert with a ratio, clamp, and put the point back at the centre of its pixel:

def _sx(self): return self.img.width() / max(self.width(), 1)

def _to_img(self, pt):                                  # widget -> image pixel
    return QPoint(min(max(int(pt.x() * self._sx()), 0), self.img.width() - 1),
                  min(max(int(pt.y() * self._sy()), 0), self.img.height() - 1))

def _to_view(self, ip):                                 # image pixel -> widget
    return QPointF((ip.x() + 0.5) / self._sx(), (ip.y() + 0.5) / self._sy())

That + 0.5 is the trick. A pixel is a square, not a point. Draw the crosshair on its corner and everything looks half a pixel off. The ruler also snaps to 45° steps with one line of atan2:

ang = round(math.atan2(dy, dx) / (math.pi / 4)) * (math.pi / 4)

Developer: int(event.x()) and hope.
Expert: knows a pixel has a centre, and that screens have scale factors.

Test 8: Can your app leave the PC exactly how it found it?

To own PrintScreen, ASNIPP has to turn off a Windows setting (PrintScreenKeyForSnippingEnabled) in the registry. That is the user's setting, not mine. So the takeover is a reversible transaction:

cur = read_prtscn_setting()
if cur != 0:
    if self.settings.get("prev_prtscn") == -1:      # remember it ONCE
        self.settings.set("prev_prtscn", cur)
    write_prtscn_setting(0)
...
# turning ASNIPP's takeover off again:
prev = self.settings.get("prev_prtscn")
if prev in (0, 1):
    write_prtscn_setting(prev)                      # put it back

Around that sit a handful of unglamorous habits that make software feel trustworthy:

  • Settings are written atomically. Write settings.json.tmp, then os.replace() over the real file. A crash mid-write can't leave half a file.
  • Settings are type-checked on load. A value is only accepted if isinstance(raw[k], type(default)). A hand-edited "autostart": "yes" can't break startup.
  • Apply first, explain second. On first run the takeover is applied before the dialog appears, so closing the box can't undo it.
  • Never show a dialog during a silent login start (--background).
  • One instance only. A named mutex, and GetLastError() == 183 (ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS) means "someone is already holding the hotkeys, so exit quietly".
  • "Start with Windows" is opt-in, and the command it writes handles Nuitka builds, PyInstaller builds and plain pythonw.exe.

Developer: ships features.
Expert: ships an undo button for every side effect.

Bonus: OCR with zero pip packages

ASNIPP can copy text out of any screenshot. No Tesseract, no model download. Windows already ships an OCR engine (Windows.Media.Ocr), and Python can drive it through PowerShell:

with open(ps1, "w", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:        # BOM so PowerShell reads Unicode correctly
    f.write(script)
subprocess.run(["powershell", "-NoProfile", "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass", "-File", ps1],
               capture_output=True, timeout=120, creationflags=0x08000000)   # no console flash

The utf-8-sig is the whole lesson: without the BOM, Windows PowerShell 5 reads the script as the legacy code page and non-English text turns to mush. And 0x08000000 (CREATE_NO_WINDOW) stops a black console from flashing on screen every time you press the button.

Also from the file: ffmpeg's atempo only accepts 0.5x to 2x, so a 4x speed-up has to be chained (atempo=2.0,atempo=2.0). A tiny while loop in atempo_chain() does it.

Try the code yourself

All of this lives in ASNIPP, built by Akhouri Systems: a pure-Python Windows app with a "Dynamic Island" style capture bar. It has no ads, no analytics and no network calls. It does exactly what's on the tin, and the hook in Test 1 only ever looks at the keys it needs.

What you get Details
📸 Photo capture Win+Shift+S, Ctrl+Shift+S or PrintScreen. Region, window or full screen, copied to clipboard and saved
🎥 Screen recorder Win+Shift+R, with system audio + mic, pause and a recording border that never appears in the video
✏️ Live drawing Ctrl+Alt+D. Pen, shapes, laser pointer and auto-fade, over any app, and it can be recorded
🎯 Colour picker + ruler Ctrl+Alt+P. Magnifier, HEX/RGB copy, pixel distances and angles
🎞️ Video editor Trim, split, join, speed, reverse, rotate, looks, GIF export
🔤 OCR + pins Copy text from any screenshot, pin an image on top of every window

👉 Download ASNIPP v1 (zip)

If you're learning how Python behaves outside a notebook, run it, press Win+Shift+S, and then ask yourself what is happening between your keypress and the screen. That is the fastest way I know to level up.

Try ASNIPP_v1:https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/ASNIPP/releases/download/v1.0.0/ASNIPP_v1.zip
not just try it, break it too.
I want feedbacks because feedbacks would make ASNIPP_v2 better.

Your score

  • 0-2 tests known: You're a Python developer. Great start. Now write something that has to talk to the OS.
  • 3-5: Solid. You've shipped something real.
  • 6-8: You're a Python expert. Come argue with me in the comments.

articles.title: x is 257 Was True on Monday and False on Tuesday
articles.description: Why Python's is and == are not the same thing, how one of them lies about numbers, and the single rule that keeps you safe.
articles.body_html:
Why Python's is and == are not the same thing, how one of them lies about numbers, and the single rule that keeps you safe.

I had a check that compared two numbers. Something close to this, simplified:

if parsed_id is expected_id:
    grant_access()

It worked. Every test passed. Then one day, with slightly different data, the same comparison started returning False for two numbers that were obviously equal. Both were 257. I printed them. They were identical. And parsed_id is expected_id was False.

So I changed the test data, and it went back to True. Smaller numbers worked. Bigger numbers did not. The comparison's correctness depended on how large the number was, which is not a sentence that should ever make sense.

The culprit was a single two-letter word I had used where I meant something else: is. In Python, is and == look interchangeable and are not. One asks "are these equal?" The other asks a completely different question, and the answer to that question happens to be unpredictable for numbers.

Here is what is actually checks, why it lied to me, and the one rule that makes this disappear.

The Two Questions Are Not the Same Question

== and is ask different things, and the whole bug lives in the gap between them.

  • == asks: are these two values equal? Do they represent the same thing? 5 == 5 is True because five equals five. This is almost always the question you actually want.
  • is asks: are these two the exact same object in memory? Not "equal," but "literally the same object, the same identity."

Two different lists that happen to hold the same items are equal but are not the same object:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]

a == b      # True  -> same contents
a is b      # False -> two different list objects

a and b are equal. They are not identical. They are two separate lists that look alike. == sees them as equal; is sees them as distinct, because they are distinct objects sitting at different places in memory.

That is the core confusion: is is not a stricter ==. It is a different operator answering a different question.

And for most values you compare, you care about equality, not identity. You want ==.

Why is Lied About My Numbers

So why did parsed_id is expected_id ever return True for 257, let alone sometimes?

Because of an optimization most people never learn about. For performance, CPython keeps a cache of small integer objects, roughly -5 through 256, created once at startup and reused everywhere. Every time you use the number 5, you get back the same cached 5 object. So for small numbers, two equal values really are the same object, and is returns True by luck.

Step outside that cached range and the luck runs out. Numbers above 256 are not cached, so two equal large numbers can be two different objects, and is returns False.

Here is the trap in its purest form, which I ran on Python 3.13:

int('256') is int('256')      # True
int('257') is int('257')      # False

Read that again. The exact same code. The only difference is 256 versus 257. One is True, the other is False, purely because 256 is in the small-integer cache and 257 is not.

That is why my check worked for small IDs and broke for large ones. is was never checking equality. It was checking identity, and identity for numbers depends on an internal caching optimization that you are not supposed to rely on and that can change between Python versions and even between how the values were produced. I had built a correctness check on top of an implementation detail.

A note, because it makes the danger worse: with plain literals written in your source (257 is 257), Python's compiler often folds them into one shared constant, so it returns True and looks fine. The failure only appears when the numbers are computed at runtime, as mine were, from parsing. So it can look correct in a quick REPL test with literals and then fail on real, computed data. Exactly the data you did not test with.

Why Python Itself Now Warns You

This mistake is common enough that recent versions of Python will warn you about one form of it. Compare a value to a literal with is and the interpreter says:

SyntaxWarning: "is" with 'str' literal. Did you mean "=="?

The language is telling you, out loud, that is is almost certainly not what you meant when comparing to a literal string or number. If you see that warning, the fix is virtually always to change is to ==. Python is trying to save you from the exact bug I shipped.

The One Place is Is Not Only Fine but Correct: None

Here is where it flips. There is a specific, important case where is is the right operator and == is subtly wrong: comparing to None.

The official Python style guide, PEP 8, states it directly:

Comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with is or is not, never the equality operators.

Always x is None, never x == None. Why? Two reasons.

First, None is a singleton. There is exactly one None object in the entire program, so "is this the same object as None" is precisely the right question, and is answers it directly and fast.

Second, and more important, == can be overridden. Any object can define its own __eq__ method and decide what it considers equal to. A badly behaved or cleverly designed object can make x == None return True when x is not actually None. I confirmed exactly this:

class Weird:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True

w = Weird()

w == None      # True   <- __eq__ hijacked the comparison
w is None      # False  <- correct: w is genuinely not None

w == None is True, which is a lie. w is None is False, which is the truth. is cannot be fooled this way, because identity is not something an object can redefine. That is why checking for None is the one case where you reach for is on purpose.

So the operators split cleanly by use case:

Comparing to... Use Why
None (and other singletons like True/False when you truly mean the object) is / is not One object exists; == can be overridden and lie
Numbers, strings, lists, any value == / != You care about equality, not identity

The Rule I Take Away

Compressed to one line:

== asks "are these equal?" is asks "are these the exact same object?" Use == for comparing values. Use is only for None and other singletons. Never use is to compare numbers or strings, because its answer depends on caching and interning you must not rely on.

The deeper lesson, the one that outlasts this specific trap, is that identity and equality are different concepts, and the two-letter word is means identity, not "equals."

English makes is feel like a synonym for equality, which is exactly why people reach for it when they mean ==. But Python's is is a precise, narrow operator about object identity, and for values like numbers that identity is governed by internal optimizations that are not part of the language's promises. Build a comparison on is for a value, and you have built it on sand that shifts between numbers, between runs, and between Python versions.

And the usual sting applies. This hides in testing because small numbers and literal values make is accidentally return True, so it looks correct right up until real, computed, larger data flows through and the identity you were never entitled to quietly stops holding.

How to Catch It Before It Catches You

Keep these four habits:

  1. Use == to compare values, always. Numbers, strings, anything where you care about the value being equal. If the question is "do these represent the same thing," that is ==, every time. Reaching for is on a value is the bug.
  2. Use is only for None and singletons. if x is None, if x is not None. This is both correct and the officially recommended style (PEP 8). The same applies if you genuinely mean the one True or False object, but for None it is essential, because == can be overridden and lie.
  3. Heed the SyntaxWarning. If Python warns "is" with a literal. Did you mean "=="?, the answer is yes, you did. Change it to ==.
  4. Never test identity-based comparisons only with small numbers or literals. is gives false confidence with cached small ints and folded literals. If you must reason about is, test with large, runtime-computed values, where the caching no longer rescues you.

I changed one is to == in that access check, and the comparison started telling the truth for every number, large or small. The two values had been equal the whole time. I had just been asking Python the wrong question, and for small numbers it had been politely giving me the right answer anyway, right up until it stopped.

The 30-Second Takeaway

  • == and is ask different questions. == asks "are these values equal?" is asks "are these the exact same object in memory?" They are not interchangeable.
  • Two equal objects can fail an is check: [1,2,3] == [1,2,3] is True, but [1,2,3] is [1,2,3] is False, because they are two distinct objects.
  • is lies about numbers because of small-integer caching. On Python 3.13: int('256') is int('256') is True (256 is cached), but int('257') is int('257') is False (257 is not). Same code, different answer by size. This is an implementation detail you must never rely on.
  • It hides in testing: small numbers and source literals make is accidentally return True (caching and compiler constant-folding). It breaks only on large, runtime-computed values.
  • The one correct use of is: None. PEP 8 says comparisons to singletons like None should always use is or is not. None is a singleton, and == can be overridden to lie (w == None can be True while w is None is False).
  • The rule: == for comparing values; is only for None and singletons; never is for numbers or strings. And if Python warns "is" with a literal, change it to ==.

Your Turn

Search your code for is and is not and check each one: is the right-hand side None (good) or a number, string, or other value (bug)? Every is comparing a value should be ==. The ones comparing to None are exactly right.

Did is vs == ever bite you in production? Tell me in the comments 👇

articles.title: getCurrentPosition() Has No Default Timeout. That's the Trap.
articles.description: A "find my location" button that works instantly on your laptop and hangs forever on a phone with a weak signal isn't flaky — it's getCurrentPosition() doing exactly what its defaults tell it to do. No timeout, no cached position, and a watcher nobody told to stop.
articles.body_html:
The ticket read: "location button sometimes just spins forever." Not a crash, not an error toast — just a spinner that never stopped. QA couldn't reproduce it. It worked every time on the office Wi-Fi, every time on a laptop, every time in the demo to the client.

It only happened out in the field. On a phone. Somewhere the GPS fix took its time and the Wi-Fi-based positioning fallback was slow to answer. Which meant it was exactly the one environment nobody tested in before shipping.

Here's the part that made it worse: the code had an error handler. Both arguments to getCurrentPosition() were filled in, success and failure. By every code-review instinct, this was handled.

The code that looks fully handled 

function useMyLocation(onFound, onFail) {
  navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
    (pos) => onFound(pos.coords),
    (err) => onFail(err.message)
  );
}

A success callback, an error callback, nothing swallowed. If you squint, it even looks defensive — most getCurrentPosition() snippets you'll find in the wild look exactly like this.

Before you keep reading: what has to happen for that error callback to fire at all? Not "what does it do" — when does the browser decide to call it?

The honest answer is: only when the browser gives up and reports a GeolocationPositionError — permission denied, position unavailable, or a timeout. And a timeout is an option you pass in. If you don't pass one, there's nothing to time out. The browser just... keeps trying. Forever, if it has to. Neither callback is under any obligation to ever run.

The default timeout is not "some reasonable number." It's Infinity.

getCurrentPosition() takes a third, optional options argument: { enableHighAccuracy, timeout, maximumAge }. Skip it — like the snippet above does — and you get the spec's own defaults:

{ enableHighAccuracy: false, timeout: Infinity, maximumAge: 0 }

timeout: Infinity means precisely what it says: the call will wait as long as the device needs to produce a position, with no upper bound. On a laptop with recent Wi-Fi positioning data cached nearby, that's near-instant, so the bug never shows up in testing. On a phone with a weak signal indoors, "as long as it needs" can be minutes — or, if the underlying location provider never calls back at all, forever. There's no silent fallback, no eventual error. The spinner you built to show while waiting just keeps being accurate.

The other default nobody reads: maximumAge: 0

maximumAge controls whether the browser is allowed to hand back a cached position instead of asking the device for a brand-new fix. The default is 0 milliseconds — meaning no cache is old enough to use, ever. Every single call to getCurrentPosition(), even one fired a hundred milliseconds after the last one, forces a fresh GPS/Wi-Fi/cell fix from scratch.

That's rarely what you actually want. A "locate me" button a user double-clicks, or a component that calls getCurrentPosition() on mount right after a sibling component just did the same thing, don't need two independent fixes a tenth of a second apart. Passing a real maximumAge — "a position up to 30 seconds old is fine" — turns repeat calls into near-free cache hits instead of two full location requests:

navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(onFound, onFail, {
  timeout: 10_000,
  maximumAge: 30_000,
});

watchPosition() has the same shape of bug as a forgotten clearInterval

getCurrentPosition() asks once. watchPosition() asks continuously, calling your success callback every time the device's position changes meaningfully — useful for live tracking, useless the moment nobody's watching the screen anymore. It returns a watch ID, and that ID is your responsibility:

const watchId = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(onMove, onError, {
  enableHighAccuracy: true,
});

// later, when you're done:
navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(watchId);

Skip that last line — the same way it's easy to skip clearInterval() — and the watch keeps running after the component that started it is gone. In a React component, that's a watchPosition() call in a useEffect with no cleanup function: the GPS radio stays active, the callback keeps firing into a component that no longer exists, and the battery drain shows up in a support ticket that has nothing to do with location on its face.

useEffect(() => {
  const id = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(onMove, onError);
  return () => navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(id);
}, []);

One line in the cleanup function. Easy to write, easy to forget, and nothing in the API warns you that you forgot it.

It's not a Promise, and that's the last gotcha

getCurrentPosition() predates fetch(), predates Promise, and was never updated to support either — it's success/error callbacks, full stop. You can't await it directly. The fix is a wrapper you write once and reuse everywhere:

function getPosition(options) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(resolve, reject, {
      enableHighAccuracy: false,
      timeout: 10_000,
      maximumAge: 30_000,
      ...options,
    });
  });
}

try {
  const pos = await getPosition();
  useLocation(pos.coords);
} catch (err) {
  if (err.code === err.PERMISSION_DENIED) showPermissionHelp();
  else if (err.code === err.TIMEOUT) showRetry();
  else showGenericError();
}

Every default that bit the original snippet is now an explicit choice, and the whole thing reads top to bottom instead of nesting two callbacks inside each other.

The one real constraint: it needs a secure origin

This part isn't a trap, just worth stating plainly: every major browser requires a secure context — HTTPS, or localhost in development — before it will even ask for location permission. That's been true for close to a decade now, not a new restriction, and there's no workaround or flag to reach for; if a getCurrentPosition() call is silently failing in a way none of the above explains, check the protocol in the address bar first.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The playground above simulates the GPS fix with a slider, so you get the exact same race every time instead of waiting on whatever signal your actual device has right now. Set a slow "fix," turn on "use the default options," and watch the stopwatch climb with nothing to stop it — that's timeout: Infinity, reproduced on demand. Then try the watchPosition() panel: start it, hit "simulate component unmount" without stopping it first, and watch the counter keep climbing anyway.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The fix for that "spins forever" ticket was three lines: a timeout, a maximumAge, and a clearWatch() in a cleanup function that had never been written. None of it was hard once someone knew to look for it — the hard part was realizing that "sometimes it just hangs" wasn't a flaky bug report. It was the spec's own default, read literally.

Does your codebase have a bare getCurrentPosition() call anywhere without a timeout? Worth a five-minute grep before it becomes someone else's "impossible to reproduce" ticket.

articles.title: Part 4: The Alert That Could Never Fire
articles.description: Since the first week of this project, observability/prometheus/alerts.yml has contained this:    -...
articles.body_html:
Since the first week of this project, observability/prometheus/alerts.yml has contained this:

- alert: PDSCircuitOpen
  expr: pybreaker_state{name="pds"} == 1

It is a correct rule. The circuit breaker in front of the Personal Demographics Service opens after five consecutive failures, the pipeline carries on with the demographics from the message, and somebody should be told.

No service has ever exported pybreaker_state. The rule has been watching a series that does not exist, which looks exactly like a healthy system.

The problem

Monitoring has a particular failure mode: you cannot tell the difference between nothing being wrong and nothing being watched. A dashboard with no red on it means one of those two things, and it does not say which.

In this pipeline, that matters more than usual, because the failures I care about mostly return 200. A patient written without an NHS number to match on is a successful request. A date of birth that failed to parse is a successful request. The breaker opening and the pipeline silently dropping to unenriched demographics is a whole shift of successful requests.

So this week I went looking for the things the pipeline does that nobody would ever find out about.

What the pipeline could not see

The breaker opens, and nothing says so

I started the transform service, sent a message, and scraped /metrics. Twenty-eight metric families, and pybreaker_state is not among them. Nothing with breaker or circuit in the name at all.

Then I drove the breaker open, which takes five failures:

breaker before      : closed | failures: 0
breaker after       : open   | failures: 5
pybreaker_state now : False

The breaker is open. The pipeline has stopped enriching. The alert cannot fire, and there is no other signal anywhere.

pybreaker makes this easy to fix. It has a CircuitBreakerListener with a state_change hook, which is called on every transition, so there is nothing to poll:

class _BreakerStateExporter(pybreaker.CircuitBreakerListener):
    def state_change(self, cb, old_state, new_state) -> None:
        BREAKER_STATE.labels(name=cb.name).set(
            _BREAKER_STATE_VALUES.get(getattr(new_state, "name", None), 0)
        )

That getattr(new_state, "name", None) is the second version. My first read new_state.state, which does not exist in pybreaker 1.2.0. The state objects carry a name instead, holding the string closed, open or half-open.

The failure mode of getting that wrong is the thing this whole article is about. getattr with a default does not raise. The lookup misses, falls back to 0, and the gauge sits there reading closed while the breaker is open. I would have shipped a fix for an unfireable alert that left it unfireable, and the metric would have existed, which is worse, because now the dashboard has a panel on it.

The test caught it.

Fields that fail to map leave no trace

Part 3 was about nine mapping defects. The reason all nine survived is in this article: only a whole-message parse failure goes to the dead-letter folder. A single field that fails to map is simply absent from the resource, and the message returns 200.

I sent a message with an unparseable date of birth:

message with an unparseable date of birth -> HTTP 200
birthDate in the resource : False
hl7_dlq_total moved?      : no
any metric for a lost field: none

The mapper now reports what it dropped, and transform turns that into
hl7_field_dropped_total{segment,field,reason}. The mapper itself stays free of Prometheus imports: it reports, the service counts. Known gaps like PID-11 and PV1-19 come through as not_mapped, so they are visible without being alarming, and unparseable_date is the one with an alert on it.

Alert rules are code that only runs during an incident

Which is the actual reason this sat here for weeks. Nothing in the build ever executed that rule.

Prometheus ships a unit test framework for alerting rules, and it took about twenty minutes to use. You give it synthetic series and assert which alerts fire and when:

- interval: 1m
  name: PDSCircuitOpen fires once the breaker is open
  input_series:
    - series: 'pybreaker_state{name="pds"}'
      values: "0x5 1x10"
  alert_rule_test:
    - eval_time: 4m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts: []
    - eval_time: 9m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts:
        - exp_labels: { severity: warning, team: interop, name: pds }

There are nine cases now. The one I would keep if I could only keep one is this:

- name: with no series exported the rule is silent, which was the bug
  input_series:
    - series: 'up{job="transform"}'
      values: "1x20"
  alert_rule_test:
    - eval_time: 15m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts: []

That is the repo as it actually stood. The rule is right, there is nothing for it to read, and the test documents that this is indistinguishable from health.

promtool check rules and promtool test rules now run as a CI job, so the rules are exercised on every pull request rather than during the first outage.

Watching it fire, rather than trusting the test

A promtool test proves the expression is right. It does not prove the pipeline produces the series under real conditions, so the last step was to break the thing on purpose:

make break-pds

That stops pds-client, sends eight messages two seconds apart, and prints the gauge after each one. Every message returns 200 throughout, which is the whole point: enrichment has stopped, the stored demographics are now whatever arrived in the message, and the front door is reporting success.

The first time I ran it against the real stack, the gauge read 0 after all eight messages. The breaker never opened.

The fix that still could not fire

The unit test for the gauge passed because it drove the breaker with an
ordinary function. The real PDS call is async, and I had wrapped it with pybreaker's decorator:

@pds_breaker
async def _call() -> dict | None:
    ...

pybreaker's only async support is for Tornado, and its README does not mention asyncio at all. On an async def function, the decorator calls it, gets a coroutine object back, and records a success. The request fails later, when the coroutine is awaited, outside the breaker. The running service had logged 16 PDS failures, and the breaker had counted none of them.

The fix is pybreaker's calling() context manager, which wraps the awaited block itself:

async def _call() -> dict | None:
    with pds_breaker.calling(), PDS_LATENCY.labels(outcome="success").time():
        resp = await http.get(...)

There is now a test that goes through the real async path with PDS failing. It fails against the old code.

It's the same shape as the getattr bug, one layer further down. The rule was right, the gauge was right, the listener was right, and the breaker they all depended on was never told anything had gone wrong. Every layer had a test and every test passed.

With the fix in, the breaker opens on the fifth message, and PDSCircuitOpen goes to Firing once the rule's two minutes have passed.

I had also worried that for: 2m could never be satisfied, because the
breaker's reset_timeout is 30 seconds and I expected the state to bounce between open and half-open. My first check of that went through the same synchronous test path, so it measured nothing real. In the running stack, the gauge held flat at 1 for twelve minutes, until I brought PDS back. pybreaker only moves to half-open when a call arrives after the timeout, and that trial call closes or reopens it in the same moment, so a ten-second scrape never sees it.

There is a second script for the other failure path, and writing it corrected something in my own plan for this article. The plan said to "stop the transform service mid-burst and show the DLQ". That does not work. The dead-letter folder is written by transform, so stopping transform means nothing writes to it at all: ingest logs the failure and answers 200 with forwarded: false. To fill the dead-letter folder you have to break what transform writes to, which is HAPI FHIR. make break-fhir does that.

Its first real run found one more. Every dead-letter write failed with
PermissionError. The service runs as an unprivileged user, and the Docker volume mounted over its dead-letter folder belonged to root, because the image never created that folder. So the messages the folder exists to keep were the ones being lost. The image now creates the folder, owned by the service user, and Docker copies it into a new volume when the volume is first created.

The panels, which I nearly forgot

Four new metrics and, for most of a day, no way to see any of them. The Grafana dashboard had six panels, and not one showed the breaker state, the dropped fields, the invalid NHS numbers or the write identity.

That is a fairly pointed thing to nearly ship in an article about not being able to see things. The series existed, and the alerts worked, and the place people actually look had not changed at all. There are ten panels now.

The one a reader found

Kevin Mayfield, who does health integration and data architecture for a living, read Part 3 and pointed out something I had not considered at all.

I had just shipped a fix that keys patient identity on the NHS number, as a conditional update. He pointed out that his trust is near the Scottish border, and that a Scottish CHI number sometimes arrives in the NHS Number field. More than that: a patient's NHS number can change when they move between the Scottish and English NHS.

Which means the identity key I had just built the whole write path around is not stable.

I tested it. Same patient, same hospital number, two messages with different NHS numbers:

message 1 request : PUT Patient?identifier=...nhs-number|1111111111
message 2 request : PUT Patient?identifier=...nhs-number|9000000009
same target?      : False
local MRN in both : L12345, L12345

Two records. The hospital number is identical in both messages and is simply not looked at. Nothing counts it, nothing alerts on it, and the FHIR server returns 200 twice.

That led somewhere I should have gone in Part 3. If the NHS number is the identity key, is it ever validated?

9000000009   checksum valid: True   accepted: True
1111111111   checksum valid: True   accepted: True
1234567890   checksum valid: False  accepted: True

No. An NHS number carries a Modulus 11 check digit, and the NHS Data Dictionary is unambiguous about it: "The check digit is validated using the Modulus 11 algorithm, and the use of this algorithm is mandatory." Multiply the first nine digits by 10 down to 2, sum, take the remainder modulo 11, and subtract from 11. A result of 11 means a check digit of 0, and "If the result is 10 then the NHS NUMBER is invalid and not used".

I was not running it. 1234567890 was being accepted as an NHS number and used to match a patient.

This is also a partial answer to Kevin's CHI point, which is why it is worth doing beyond tidiness. A CHI number is also ten digits, and it will not satisfy the NHS check digit. So a sending system supplying CHI numbers in the NHS Number field now shows up as a rate on nhs_number_invalid_total rather than as silently mismatched patients.

An identifier that fails the check is still kept on the resource, because the sender sent it and dropping it loses information. It is just never used to look a patient up or to match an existing record. A wrong identity is worse than no identity.

Writes with nothing to match on are now counted as patient_write_total{identity="none"}, and there is an alert when that passes a tenth of writes.

What none of this catches

The thing Kevin actually described is not a metric problem.

Counting writes with no identity tells you when matching is degrading. It does not tell you that the same person has arrived twice under two different NHS numbers, because from inside a single message that looks completely normal. Both messages are valid, both have good check digits, both write successfully.

Catching that needs a matching step, which is what he does:

I have a scoring system based on identifier, date of birth, gender, name and postcode. I weight MRN and NHS the highest, then DOB.

A demographic query first, then a weighted score across several fields, rather than trusting one identifier. He also raised the fetus and baby case, where a newborn may not have its own NHS number yet, which breaks identifier-first matching in a different direction.

That is a substantial piece of work, and it is not in this week's change. What this week does is make the conditions that feed it visible, so when the matching goes in there is something to measure it against.

Worth stealing

Test your alert rules. They are the only code in the repo that runs exclusively during an incident, which makes them the least exercised and the most load-bearing. promtool test rules exists and takes an afternoon to adopt.

Assert the series exists, not just that the rule is right. My rule was correct the whole time. The failure was one level below it, and no amount of reviewing the expression would have found it.

Watch for silent fallbacks in monitoring code: getattr with a default, or a synchronous decorator around an async function. Both fail by doing nothing, in the thing that is supposed to tell you about silent failures. My gauge read zero for the same reason the alert read quiet.

Count the successes you are unsure about. Error rates are the easy half. patient_write_total{identity="none"} counts requests that returned 200 and did something I would rather they had not.

Export the metric and add the panel in the same change. I had the series, the alert and the rule test before I noticed the dashboard still showed the same six panels it had in week one. A metric nobody has a graph for is halfway back to where this started.

Where AI helps here, and where it doesn't

I built this project with Claude Code. This week I had it write the metrics, the promtool tests and the break scripts, then made it prove each one against the running stack, not the code.

Writing the listener, the metrics and the promtool cases was quick. The useful part was the step before: starting the service, scraping /metrics and reading the list of what was actually there, rather than reading the alert file and the service code and believing they lined up. They had not lined up for weeks, and both halves looked correct on their own.

It also wrote the async decorator bug, and the first timing check that went through the same synchronous path. Both were caught the same way, by running the real stack and reading what it did.

Four weeks in, the pattern is stable enough to state plainly. Every finding in this series has come from running the thing, and the two most valuable have come from people who read it and knew more than I did about the domain. Neither of those is a code review.

What I'd do differently

I would have written the alert rule tests at the same time as the alert rules, in the first week. Not because the rules were wrong, but because writing the test is what forces you to produce the series, and producing the series is what I had skipped.

I would also have written the break scripts first. make break-pds is about thirty lines, and it is the only thing here that tests the whole chain, from a stopped container through to a rule evaluating in Prometheus. Everything else in this article tests one layer and assumes the next one. I would also have run it before tagging this part, not after.

And I would have remembered that fixing the code does not fix the data it already wrote. The demo database held 996 copies of the same test patient from before Part 3's conditional update. The conditional update then refused, correctly, to pick one, with the 412 the FHIR spec requires. I reset the demo database. A trust can't, and that is where the matching work Kevin described begins.

Sources

  • NHS Data Dictionary: NHS NUMBER, including the Modulus 11 check
  • Prometheus: unit testing rules
  • Prometheus: alerting rules
  • pybreaker on PyPI
  • pybreaker README: the calling() context manager and Tornado-only async support
  • FHIR R4: conditional update, including the 412 on multiple matches
  • Docker: populating a volume from a container
  • prometheus_client for Python
  • The code for this article, tag part-4

Next

Part 5, on 11 November, is security and compliance, which has a backlog of its own: two documents in this repo describe a DataClass tag applied by a Terraform block that is commented out.

Which of your alert rules has never fired, and do you know whether that is good news?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

articles.title: 133,334 Projections for 66,667 Receipts
articles.description: A Count() I added for a log line was re-running my whole LINQ query. I made the projection count itself to catch the double enumeration, then fixed it in one line.
articles.body_html:
A reporting method on a dashboard endpoint started showing up in the traces twice as heavy as the numbers it returned could explain. It pulled a filtered set of orders, logged how many there were, then summed them. Two cheap-sounding operations. The profiler disagreed, and the line it kept landing on was the one I'd never have circled: a Count() call I'd added for a log message.

Here's the shape of what I had.

void Report(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} receipts", receipts.Count());

    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in receipts)
        total += r.Total;

    logger.LogInformation("Total {Total:C}", total);
}

Looks like it touches the data twice, which it does, but that's not the expensive part. The expensive part is where receipts came from. It wasn't a list. It was a LINQ pipeline someone handed down the call chain:

var receipts = orders
    .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
    .Select(o => new Receipt(o.Id, double.Parse(o.RawAmount) * 1.2));

That expression doesn't contain any receipts. It's a recipe for producing them, and it produces them fresh every single time something enumerates it. Count() enumerates it once to count. The foreach enumerates it again to sum. Same recipe, run top to bottom twice, filter and parse and allocate on both passes. The log line I thought was free was re-running the entire query.

Making the query admit it

I didn't want to argue from the profiler's vibe, so I made the projection count itself. Every time the Select runs, it bumps a counter. If the pipeline runs twice, the counter can't hide it.

int projected = 0;

IEnumerable<Receipt> Pipeline(IEnumerable<Order> orders) =>
    orders
        .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
        .Select(o =>
        {
            Interlocked.Increment(ref projected);
            var amount = double.Parse(o.RawAmount);
            return new Receipt(o.Id, amount * 1.2);
        });

Then I ran the two-pass consumer against it and compared it to the obvious fix: enumerate once into a List, then ask the list whatever you want. Two hundred thousand source rows, a third of them in the EU bucket, so 66,667 matches. Best of seven, JIT warmed first. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I trust the projection count (it's exact) more than the millisecond.

// two passes: Count() then foreach, straight off the pipeline
var count = receipts.Count();
double total = 0;
foreach (var r in receipts) total += r.Total;

// one pass: materialize, then count and sum the list
var list = receipts.ToList();
double total = 0;
foreach (var r in list) total += r.Total;

Source rows:        200,000
EU rows (expected): 66,667
Results agree:      True (66,667 receipts)

enumerate twice  projections:    133,334   best:    12.2 ms
materialize once projections:     66,667   best:     7.2 ms

Projection ratio: 2.00x
Time ratio:       1.69x

Exactly double. 133,334 projections to produce 66,667 receipts, because every receipt got built, filtered, and parsed twice and half of them thrown away the first time around. The wall clock didn't quite double, which is the honest part: parsing and allocating are most of the cost here but not all of it, so the second pass adds about two-thirds again rather than a clean 100%. The ratio you'll see depends entirely on how heavy your Select is. Mine's a double.Parse. If yours hits a database, "twice" stops being a benchmark curiosity and becomes two round trips.

The fix is one call, and so is the trap

Materializing with ToList() collapses it back to one pass. The consumer can count the list, enumerate the list, index into the list, all for free, because a List<T> is results, not a recipe. If a method is going to look at a sequence more than once, it should own a materialized copy rather than a lazy expression it doesn't control.

The caveat, and it's a real one: ToList() is also how you turn a lovely streaming, bounded-memory pipeline into a full buffer in RAM. If the sequence is huge, or infinite, or you're deliberately streaming it so you never hold all of it at once, materializing is the bug and single-pass enumeration is the feature. The honest rule I land on is about intent. If I'm going to touch a sequence exactly once, left to right, I leave it lazy.
